Major tea-growing countries.China: China is the birthplace of tea and still the largest producer, making white, green, oolong, black, yellow and dark teas.
Major tea-growing countries.India: India is the world's second-biggest tea producer, and Darjeeling and Assam are among its famous growing regions.
Major tea-growing countries.Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka's tea is still sold as Ceylon, the country's old colonial name, and it started when a coffee blight wiped out the plantations.
Major tea-growing countries.Kenya: Kenya is the world's top exporter of black tea, and most of it grows on smallholder farms in the highlands.
Major tea-growing countries.Japan: Japan grows mostly green tea, including matcha, where the plants are shaded for weeks before harvest to boost flavor.
Major tea-growing countries.Vietnam: Vietnam is among the top tea exporters, and its mountain regions produce much of the world's green and lotus-scented tea.
Major tea-growing countries.Indonesia: Indonesia grows tea on the cool slopes of Java and Sumatra, a legacy of Dutch colonial plantations.
Major tea-growing countries.Turkey: Turkey surprises many: it is one of the biggest tea producers and drinkers, with leaves grown on the damp Black Sea coast near Rize.
Major tea-growing countries.Iran: Iran grows tea along the Caspian coast and is a huge drinker of it, often served from a samovar with sugar cubes.
Major tea-growing countries.Bangladesh: Bangladesh's tea gardens in Sylhet are among the world's lushest, and the country is a significant producer of black tea.
Major tea-growing countries.Malawi: Malawi was the first African country to grow tea commercially, starting in the late 1800s, and still exports it widely.
Major tea-growing countries.United Kingdom: Britons drink some of the world's heaviest tea, but Britain's climate isn't suited to it; almost all is imported, apart from a few tiny estates.
Major tea-growing countries.Ireland: The Irish drink more tea per person than almost anyone, yet it all arrives from abroad as the climate is wrong for the plant.
Major tea-growing countries.Morocco: Morocco is famous for sweet mint tea poured from a height, but the tea leaves are imported from China.
Major tea-growing countries.Egypt: Egyptians drink plenty of tea, called shai, but the crop doesn't thrive in the arid climate, so it is imported.
Major tea-growing countries.Canada: Canada has a few tiny tea farms, such as one on Vancouver Island, but it produces next to nothing commercially.
Major tea-growing countries.Germany: East Frisia in Germany drinks more tea per head than almost anywhere, but the leaves are all imported.
Major tea-growing countries.Netherlands: The Dutch were early tea importers into Europe, but cannot grow the plant at home, only trade it.
Major tea-growing countries.Saudi Arabia: Saudi Arabia drinks lots of tea and coffee, but its desert has no climate for growing tea.
Major tea-growing countries.Sweden: Sweden is a heavy coffee nation and imports its tea; the plant can't handle the long northern winters.
Major tea-growing countries.Poland: Poles drink a lot of tea, famously in glasses, but the leaves are imported and the climate rules out growing it.
Major tea-growing countries.Mexico: Mexico is better known for coffee and agave, and it produces almost no commercial tea.
Major tea-growing countries.Libya: Libyans serve a strong, foamy tea in small glasses, but the country is too dry to grow any.
Major tea-growing countries.Iceland: Icelandic geothermal greenhouses can grow bananas, but commercial tea is not grown there.

Foods that are toxic to dogs.Chocolate: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs process slowly. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are the most dangerous.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Grapes: Grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, yet vets still don't know the exact toxin. Some dogs react to a few, others to many.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Raisins: Dried grapes are even more concentrated, and a small handful can be dangerous to a small dog. The toxic compound remains a mystery.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Onions: Onions damage dogs' red blood cells and can cause anemia. Cooked, raw or powdered, they all count, including in baby food.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Garlic: Garlic is part of the same plant family as onions and harms dogs the same way, though it is stronger, ounce for ounce.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Xylitol: A sugar substitute in sugar-free gum and some peanut butter. In dogs it triggers a sharp insulin release and can cause liver failure.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Macadamia nuts: Macadamias can make dogs weak, shaky and feverish, even in small amounts. The reason isn't fully understood.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Alcohol: Dogs are far more sensitive than people. Even a small amount of beer or unbaked bread dough, which makes alcohol as it rises, can harm them.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Coffee: Caffeine is a stimulant that dogs can't handle well. Coffee grounds and beans are a hazard, and tea and cola can be too.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Chives: Chives are in the onion family, so they carry the same risk of damaging a dog's red blood cells.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Leeks: Leeks are relatives of onions and garlic, and carry the same threat to a dog's red blood cells.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Carrots: Safe and crunchy. Raw carrots can help clean teeth a little, and frozen ones soothe teething puppies.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Plain rice: Plain boiled rice is a vet favorite for upset stomachs, usually served with chicken.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Blueberries: A safe treat for dogs, packed with antioxidants. Many owners freeze them for a crunchy snack.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Pumpkin: Plain cooked pumpkin is full of fiber, and vets often suggest it for dogs with mild digestive upset.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Cooked chicken: Plain cooked chicken is safe and popular, as long as bones are removed since cooked bones can splinter.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Green beans: Safe, low-calorie, and often used by vets to help overweight dogs feel full.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Banana: Banana is safe in moderation, and rich in potassium. It's high in sugar, so slices should stay a treat.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Sweet potato: Safe when cooked and plain. They're rich in fiber and beta-carotene, which is why they show up in dog foods.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Cucumber: Cucumbers are about 95 percent water and low in calories, making them a safe, hydrating snack for dogs.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Cooked salmon: Cooked salmon is safe and rich in omega-3s. Raw salmon is the problem, as it can carry a parasite that makes dogs very sick.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Apple slices: Apple flesh is safe, but the seeds contain a tiny amount of cyanide-releasing compound. Remove the core before sharing.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Plain oatmeal: Plain cooked oats are fine for dogs and gentle on the stomach. It's the sugar, raisins or xylitol-sweetened extras that cause trouble.
Foods that are toxic to dogs.Zucchini: Zucchini is safe for dogs, and low in calories. Unlike some squash relatives, the kind in shops is not bitter or toxic.

Bitter foods and drinks.Coffee: Bitterness in coffee comes from compounds like caffeine and chlorogenic acids, and roasting changes them. We learn to like it, since babies reject it.
Bitter foods and drinks.Dark chocolate: Cocoa solids contain flavanols and theobromine, both bitter. Higher percentages mean less sugar and more bite.
Bitter foods and drinks.Grapefruit: Its bitterness comes from naringin, found in the white pith. Grapefruit can also interfere with a number of medications.
Bitter foods and drinks.Bitter melon: A gourd used in Asian cooking whose name is a warning. Cooks soak or salt it to tame its bitterness, which comes from compounds like momordicin.
Bitter foods and drinks.Endive: Its bitterness comes from compounds in the leaves. Belgian endive is grown in the dark to keep it pale and milder.
Bitter foods and drinks.Radicchio: A ruby-red Italian chicory that tastes bitter raw. Grilling or roasting mellows it and brings out some sweetness.
Bitter foods and drinks.Tonic water: The bitterness is quinine, from cinchona bark, once used to fight malaria. The gin and tonic grew from British colonial drinkers in India.
Bitter foods and drinks.Dandelion greens: These common lawn weeds are eaten as a bitter green, and people blanch them to soften their sharpness. Young leaves are milder.
Bitter foods and drinks.Cocoa nibs: Crushed roasted cocoa beans with no added sugar. They're crunchy, intensely chocolatey and bitter.
Bitter foods and drinks.Espresso: Despite its reputation, a well-pulled espresso shouldn't be harshly bitter. A short, fast extraction balances sweetness, acid and bitterness.
Bitter foods and drinks.Campari: The bright red Italian aperitif has been made since 1860. Its bitterness comes from herbs and fruit, and it's the key to a Negroni.
Bitter foods and drinks.Honey: Naturally sweet, produced by bees from nectar. It never really spoils, as jars sealed in tombs have been found edible.
Bitter foods and drinks.Banana: Sweet, with sugar rising as it ripens. No notable bitterness, aside from the peel.
Bitter foods and drinks.Sugar: The standard of sweetness. Sugar also cancels bitterness, so we add it to coffee and tea.
Bitter foods and drinks.Maple syrup: Sweet sap boiled down at a ratio of about 40 parts sap to 1 of syrup.
Bitter foods and drinks.Watermelon: Sweet and watery, with no real bitter notes. The white rind near the skin is a little bitter, but the red flesh is sweet.
Bitter foods and drinks.Strawberry: Sweet and slightly tart, not bitter. Botanically, the seeds on the outside are the actual fruits.
Bitter foods and drinks.Mango: Ripe mango is sweet and lush. Related to cashews and pistachios, it carries a sap that can irritate skin like poison ivy.
Bitter foods and drinks.Milk: Milk is mildly sweet thanks to lactose, its natural sugar. It also tames bitterness, which is why people add it to tea and coffee.
Bitter foods and drinks.Vanilla ice cream: Creamy and sweet, and vanilla itself is a spice that comes from an orchid pod. It's one of the costliest spices in the world.
Bitter foods and drinks.Caramel: A trap, since burnt caramel turns bitter. Properly made, though, it's rich and sweet, with just a bitter edge.
Bitter foods and drinks.Cotton candy: Nothing but sugar, so sweet it's almost all you taste. A bitter note would mean it burned.
Bitter foods and drinks.Peach: Sweet and juicy. The pit and its kernel contain compounds that can be bitter, and shouldn't be eaten.
Bitter foods and drinks.Marshmallow: Sugar, air and gelatin make for a purely sweet and soft treat, with no bitterness.

Not actually the animal their name ends.Starfish: Starfish are echinoderms, related to sea urchins, with no brain or blood. Many can regrow lost arms, so biologists prefer 'sea star'.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Jellyfish: Jellyfish are made of about 95 percent water and have no brain, heart or bones. They've drifted in the oceans for over 500 million years.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Koala bear: Koalas are marsupials, not bears. Their closest relatives are wombats, and a baby koala spends months in its mother's pouch.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Guinea pig: Guinea pigs come from the Andes, not Guinea, and aren't pigs. They're rodents, and in Peru they are still eaten as cuy.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Sea lion: Sea lions are eared seals, related to bears and dogs, not lions. Unlike true seals they can rotate their hind flippers to walk on land.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Prairie dog: Prairie dogs are ground squirrels, not dogs. They have a complex 'language' of barks that can describe a predator's size and colour.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Flying fox: The flying fox is a big fruit bat, not a fox. Some species have wingspans of about 1.5 metres.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Electric eel: The electric eel is a knifefish, closer to catfish than true eels. It can produce a shock of up to about 600 volts.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Horned toad: The horned toad is actually a lizard, not a toad. When really alarmed, it can squirt blood from its eyes.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Mountain lion: The mountain lion is also known as the cougar, puma or panther, and has more names than any other mammal. It's not a true lion.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Silverfish: Silverfish are wingless insects, not fish. They've existed for about 400 million years, and can survive for a year without eating.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Seahorse: Seahorses are fish, with a fin and gills, though they look nothing like fish. The horse part is just their head shape.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Tiger shark: The tiger shark is a real shark. Its name comes from the dark stripes juveniles carry, which fade with age.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Sea turtle: The sea turtle is a real turtle, a reptile. Females return to their birth beaches to lay eggs, after years at sea.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Arctic fox: The Arctic fox is a real fox, and its coat changes from white to brown with the seasons. It can survive temperatures near minus 50 degrees Celsius.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Fruit bat: The fruit bat is a real bat. Many are important pollinators and seed spreaders, vital for tropical forests.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Barn owl: The barn owl is a real owl, with the heart-shaped face. It can locate prey in total darkness by sound alone.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Honeybee: The honeybee is a real bee. A hive might hold up to about 50,000 bees, and a single worker visits thousands of flowers a day.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Clownfish: The clownfish is a real fish. All are born male, and the dominant one in a group can turn female.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Snow goose: The snow goose is a real goose. Huge flocks fly in V formations, which save energy for the birds behind.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Grizzly bear: The grizzly is a real bear, a subspecies of the brown bear. Its name probably refers to grizzled, silver-tipped fur.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Humpback whale: The humpback is a real whale. Males sing complex songs that can be heard for many kilometres, and that evolve over time.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Bullfrog: The bullfrog is a real frog. The American bullfrog's call can be heard from a long distance, and it's an invasive pest in many places.
Not actually the animal their name ends.Catfish: The catfish is a real fish, with whisker-like barbels. These are packed with taste buds, and some species taste with their whole body.

Desert plants.Saguaro: The saguaro is the giant cactus of the Sonoran Desert. It may take 50 to 75 years to grow its first arm, and it can live for 150 to 200 years.
Desert plants.Joshua tree: The Joshua tree is a yucca, not a true tree. Its name is credited to Mormon settlers, who saw its arms as Joshua's raised hands.
Desert plants.Agave: Agave stores water in its fleshy leaves, and blooms only once at the end of its life. The century plant doesn't really take 100 years, but may take decades.
Desert plants.Prickly pear: The prickly pear is a cactus whose paddles and fruit are both eaten. It's a staple of Mexican cuisine, where the paddles are called nopales.
Desert plants.Creosote bush: The creosote bush gives off a rain-like smell after desert showers. Some clonal rings are estimated to be over 10,000 years old.
Desert plants.Yucca: Yucca is a desert shrub with a symbiotic partner: each species is pollinated by its own yucca moth. Neither can reproduce without the other.
Desert plants.Barrel cactus: The barrel cactus is round with ribs that expand to store water. Despite the legend, drinking its pulp is not a safe source of water.
Desert plants.Ocotillo: The ocotillo looks like dead sticks for most of the year, and sprouts leaves within days after rain. Hummingbirds visit its red flowers.
Desert plants.Welwitschia: Welwitschia lives in the Namib Desert, and grows just two leaves for its whole life. It can live well over 1,000 years.
Desert plants.Date palm: The date palm thrives in desert oases, with deep roots reaching groundwater. Dates have been cultivated for thousands of years.
Desert plants.Mesquite: Mesquite has roots that can reach deeper than 50 metres to groundwater. Its seed pods were ground into flour by native peoples.
Desert plants.Tumbleweed: Tumbleweeds break off and roll with the wind to scatter their seeds. The classic Western kind is actually the Russian thistle, from Eurasia.
Desert plants.Fern: Ferns need damp shade to grow, in conditions the desert lacks. Their ancestors thrived in swampy forests over 300 million years ago.
Desert plants.Moss: Moss lacks true roots and dries out easily, so prefers moist places. Yet some mosses can survive in deserts by going dormant.
Desert plants.Water lily: The water lily needs still water to survive, so the desert is no home. Its seeds can survive dry spells for years, though.
Desert plants.Bamboo: Bamboo thrives in humid, warm regions with ample water. It's a grass, and some species flower only once every 100 years.
Desert plants.Rhododendron: The rhododendron likes acidic, damp soils and cool, misty woods. Nepal's national flower is a rhododendron.
Desert plants.Maple: Maple trees prefer temperate, moist forests. Their sap is boiled down at roughly 40 to 1 to make syrup.
Desert plants.Lotus: The lotus needs standing water, so it doesn't belong in a desert. Its leaves repel water and dirt, an effect called self-cleaning.
Desert plants.Rice: Rice grows in flooded paddies and is the opposite of a desert plant. It feeds roughly half the world's population.
Desert plants.Cattail: The cattail grows in wet marshes and ponds. It can't survive dry deserts, though it's a hardy colonist of ditches.
Desert plants.Hosta: The hosta is a shade-loving garden plant that needs moisture. Slugs and deer love it, which gardeners know well.
Desert plants.Willow: Willows grow near water, and their roots go looking for it. Willow bark was an early source of salicin, a forerunner of aspirin.
Desert plants.Venus flytrap: The Venus flytrap grows in the boggy, nutrient-poor soils of the Carolinas. It snaps shut in about a tenth of a second, but only after two touches.

Things associated with Scotland.Kilts: Traditionally worn with a sporran, since kilts have no pockets; the pleated style is meant to be worn in the clan's own tartan.
Things associated with Scotland.Bagpipes: The Great Highland pipes are loud enough to be heard miles away, which is why clans once used them to rally fighters in battle.
Things associated with Scotland.Haggis: Sheep offal, oats and spices cooked in a stomach casing, and honored each January 25 on Burns Night with a poem addressed to it.
Things associated with Scotland.Tartan: Each clan pattern is called a sett, and the Scottish Register of Tartans lists thousands of registered designs.
Things associated with Scotland.Nessie: The Loch Ness Monster's fame took off in 1933, and the loch is deep enough to hold more water than all the lakes of England and Wales.
Things associated with Scotland.Highland games: Gatherings of athletics and music where heavy events like the hammer throw and stone put test raw strength, often with pipe bands playing.
Things associated with Scotland.Shortbread: Its name comes from the high butter content that makes it crumbly, or 'short'; it is a traditional Hogmanay and Christmas treat.
Things associated with Scotland.Caber toss: Athletes flip a log up to about 6 meters long end over end; judges score the throw by how straight it lands, not by distance.
Things associated with Scotland.Thistle: Scotland's national flower. Legend says a barefoot Norse raider cried out stepping on one, alerting sleeping Scots to the attack.
Things associated with Scotland.Hogmanay: The Scots' New Year celebration is often bigger than Christmas, with first-footing: the first visitor over the threshold should bring gifts like coal.
Things associated with Scotland.Irn-Bru: This bright orange soft drink outsells Coca-Cola in Scotland, which is a rare feat for a local brand.
Things associated with Scotland.Scotch whisky: By law it must be matured in oak casks in Scotland for at least three years, and many bottlings age much longer.
Things associated with Scotland.Leprechauns: These mischievous shoemaker fairies come from Irish folklore, and they are said to hide pots of gold at the end of rainbows.
Things associated with Scotland.Shamrock: Ireland's three-leaf clover is tied to St. Patrick, who supposedly used it to explain the Trinity; the thistle is Scotland's emblem instead.
Things associated with Scotland.Guinness: The stout was brewed in Dublin, not Scotland, and Arthur Guinness famously signed a 9,000-year lease on the brewery site in 1759.
Things associated with Scotland.Leek: A national emblem of Wales, supposedly worn by Welsh soldiers in battle to tell friend from foe; it has nothing to do with Scotland.
Things associated with Scotland.Daffodil: Another Welsh emblem, partly because the Welsh word for leek, cennin, is close to the word for daffodil, cennin Pedr.
Things associated with Scotland.Eisteddfod: A Welsh festival of poetry, music and performance whose roots go back to the twelfth century; the Scottish equivalent is called a Mod.
Things associated with Scotland.Morris dancing: An English folk tradition, with dancers wearing bells and waving handkerchiefs or sticks, and nothing to do with Scotland.
Things associated with Scotland.Clogs: Wooden shoes are linked to the Netherlands and parts of northern England, not Scotland, where ghillie brogues go with Highland dress.
Things associated with Scotland.Lederhosen: Leather shorts from Bavaria and Austria, famously worn at Oktoberfest, not the kilt country of the Highlands.
Things associated with Scotland.Stonehenge: This stone circle stands on England's Salisbury Plain and was built in stages starting about 5,000 years ago; Scotland's counterpart is Callanish.
Things associated with Scotland.Riverdance: The Irish step-dance show began as a seven-minute interval act at the 1994 Eurovision Song Contest before becoming a worldwide hit.
Things associated with Scotland.Tulips: Tulips make people think of the Netherlands, where the flower mania of the 1630s saw single bulbs sell for the price of a house.

National capitals in the Middle East.Riyadh: Saudi Arabia's capital grew from a walled desert town into a metropolis of several million in under a century, thanks to oil wealth.
National capitals in the Middle East.Baghdad: Founded in 762 as a circular city, it became the center of Abbasid learning, where scholars at the House of Wisdom translated Greek science.
National capitals in the Middle East.Tehran: It lies beneath the snowy Alborz range, so ski slopes sit within an hour's drive of the city; Iran's capital since the late 1700s.
National capitals in the Middle East.Amman: Jordan's capital spreads over hills and, in ancient times, was called Philadelphia after a Ptolemaic king.
National capitals in the Middle East.Beirut: Long nicknamed the 'Paris of the Middle East', Lebanon's capital has been destroyed and rebuilt many times over thousands of years.
National capitals in the Middle East.Damascus: Among the oldest continuously inhabited cities, it gave its name to damask fabric and, according to tradition, Damascus steel.
National capitals in the Middle East.Muscat: Oman's capital is home to the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, which holds an enormous hand-woven carpet that took years to make.
National capitals in the Middle East.Doha: Qatar's capital hosted the 2022 FIFA World Cup final, and its Museum of Islamic Art sits on a purpose-built island.
National capitals in the Middle East.Kuwait City: Most of Kuwait's population lives in or around the capital, whose Kuwait Towers are a national symbol.
National capitals in the Middle East.Abu Dhabi: The capital of the UAE is not Dubai but Abu Dhabi, which holds most of the federation's oil and the huge Sheikh Zayed Mosque.
National capitals in the Middle East.Manama: The Bahraini capital sits on an island nation once famed for its pearl divers before oil replaced pearls.
National capitals in the Middle East.Dubai: Dubai is the largest UAE city and home of the Burj Khalifa, but the capital is Abu Dhabi.
National capitals in the Middle East.Jeddah: Jeddah is Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port and the gateway for pilgrims heading to Mecca, but the capital is Riyadh.
National capitals in the Middle East.Mecca: Islam's holiest city, which draws millions of pilgrims for the hajj, is a religious center, not Saudi Arabia's capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Medina: Medina holds the Prophet's Mosque and is Islam's second-holiest city, but the Saudi capital is Riyadh.
National capitals in the Middle East.Basra: Iraq's main port and oil hub on the Shatt al-Arab waterway is a major city, but Baghdad is the capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Istanbul: Turkey straddles Europe and Asia and Istanbul was the Ottoman capital until 1923, but today's capital is Ankara.
National capitals in the Middle East.Isfahan: Isfahan was the glittering Safavid capital in the 1500s and 1600s, and its Naqsh-e Jahan Square was boasted to be 'half the world'.
National capitals in the Middle East.Aleppo: Syria's largest city for years is one of the world's oldest inhabited places, with a giant covered souq, but not the capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Petra: Petra is a rock-cut Nabataean city in Jordan, famed for the Treasury carved into pink cliffs, not a modern capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Mosul: Mosul is Iraq's northern city, near the ruins of ancient Nineveh, but Baghdad is the capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Shiraz: Shiraz is a city of poets, Hafez and Saadi are buried here, and Persepolis lies nearby, but Tehran is Iran's capital.
National capitals in the Middle East.Salalah: Oman's southern city is known for its monsoon season, the khareef, and for frankincense, but the capital is Muscat.
National capitals in the Middle East.Aqaba: Aqaba is Jordan's only seaport, on the Red Sea, but it isn't the capital; Amman is.

Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Bunsen burner: Chemist Robert Bunsen popularized this burner in the 1850s, though his lab assistant Peter Desaga built the design.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Test tubes: Test tubes give any scientist-lab a classic look, and are often made from heat-resistant borosilicate glass.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Beaker: Beaker markings are only approximations, so serious measuring uses a graduated cylinder.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Tesla coil: Nikola Tesla invented this resonant transformer around 1891 to produce high-voltage sparks.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Lab coat: The white lab coat took off in the late 1800s as doctors tried to look scientific and clean.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Goggles: Safety goggles protect eyes from splashes, and mad scientists are rarely seen wearing them.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Petri dish: The Petri dish is named for Julius Petri, who worked for Robert Koch in 1887.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Microscope: A microscope lets a scientist see cells and microbes, first glimpsed in the 1600s.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Bubbling potion: Movie potions bubble because of dry ice or heat, and the neon glow is just effects.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Lightning rod: Benjamin Franklin devised the lightning rod in the 1750s, and films use lightning to give monsters life.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Brain in a jar: The brain in a jar echoes the philosophical 'brain in a vat' thought experiment that Hilary Putnam popularized in 1981.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Erlenmeyer flask: The Erlenmeyer flask is named for the German chemist Emil Erlenmeyer, who designed it in 1860.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Centrifuge: A centrifuge spins samples at thousands of revolutions per minute to separate substances like blood components.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Beach umbrella: The beach umbrella is for shade, and umbrellas began as sun shades in ancient times.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Surfboard: Surfboards come from ancient Polynesians, who surfed on wooden boards.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Wedding cake: A popular story says the tiered wedding cake was modeled on the steeple of St Bride's Church in London.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Lawn mower: Edwin Budding invented the lawn mower in England in 1830 to trim sports grounds.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Tuba: The tuba was invented in Berlin in 1835 and is the lowest-pitched brass instrument.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Trampoline: George Nissen built the trampoline in the 1930s, inspired by circus performers' safety nets.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Hammock: The Taíno people of the Caribbean made the first hammocks, and sailors adopted them.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Bowling ball: Bowling balls were once made of wood before rubber and plastic took over.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Kayak: The kayak was invented by the Inuit, who covered its frame with seal skin.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Garden gnome: Garden gnomes first appeared in Germany in the 1800s.
Things a mad scientist would keep in the.Pogo stick: Pogo-stick patents date to the early 1920s, a craze of that decade.

Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Fossils: The word comes from Latin for dug up. Most fossils form when minerals slowly replace the bones or shells of buried organisms.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Dinosaur bones: Dinosaur bones are rarely bone any more; over millions of years minerals turn them into stone that keeps their structure.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Ammonites: These coiled shells of extinct cephalopods vanished with the dinosaurs, and Whitby's coat of arms features them as snakestones.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Trilobites: Armored sea creatures that lived for about 270 million years, and had some of the first complex eyes with crystal lenses.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Insects in amber: Resin hardened over millions of years preserved insects in fine detail, which inspired the idea behind Jurassic Park.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Fossil footprints: Trackways show how animals moved; at Laetoli in Tanzania, 3.6-million-year-old footprints show early human relatives walking upright.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Coprolites: Fossilized dung, which sounds gross but reveals what extinct animals ate, including bone fragments from a T. rex meal.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Petrified wood: Not wood anymore: minerals like silica replaced the cells one by one, keeping tree rings visible in solid stone.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Mammoth tusks: Frozen in Siberia, they are still traded as ivory, and growth layers can tell scientists about the animal's life.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Fossil shark teeth: Sharks shed thousands of teeth in a lifetime, which is why their teeth are among the most common fossils found.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Pottery: A trap: broken pots are archaeology's bread and butter, because human-made styles help date a site.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Ancient coins: A trap: coins are made by people, so they belong to archaeology, and rulers' faces on them help pin down dates.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Mummies: A trap: Egyptian mummies are archaeology, as the preserved bodies were deliberately made by humans, though natural mummies like Otzi also exist.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Arrowheads: A trap: shaped by human hands from stone, they are archaeological finds even though the stone itself is natural.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Roman mosaics: A trap: tiny stone tiles laid by craftsmen are artifacts of human culture, so they fit archaeology rather than paleontology.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Viking swords: A trap: these are tools made by people, and some had the maker's name, Ulfberht, inlaid in the blade.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Cave paintings: A trap: made by humans, which makes them archaeology; some in Indonesia are over 40,000 years old.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Gold nuggets: A trap: nuggets are minerals, not human-made nor once alive, so neither field really studies them; geologists do.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Ancient scrolls: A trap: writing is a human artifact, so scrolls belong to archaeology, like the Dead Sea Scrolls found in desert caves.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Terracotta warriors: A trap: thousands of clay soldiers buried with China's first emperor are archaeology, and each face is slightly different.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Diamonds: A trap: they are minerals formed deep in Earth, so geology covers them. Never fossils, they are pure carbon.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Pharaoh's tomb: A trap: tombs are human construction, so archaeology, and Tutankhamun's was found nearly intact in 1922.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Shipwrecks: A trap: sunken ships are human-made, so the field is maritime archaeology, though ancient ones can be thousands of years old.
Paleontology finds (not archaeology).Totem pole: A trap: carved by Pacific Northwest peoples, these belong to cultural heritage and archaeology, not to the study of ancient life.

Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Visible light: Only a sliver of the spectrum, roughly 380 to 750 nanometres, is visible to human eyes; everything else here is the same thing, just invisible.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Radio waves: Same speed as light, yet a command to Mars still needs anywhere from about 3 to 22 minutes to arrive, depending on the planets' positions.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.X-rays: Röntgen found them in 1895 while testing a tube, and X-rayed his wife's hand; the X stood for unknown, and he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Gravitational waves: Ripples in spacetime that travel at light speed; LIGO first caught them in 2015, from two black holes that merged over a billion years ago.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Microwaves: The cosmic microwave background is the Big Bang's afterglow, light released when the universe was about 380,000 years old and still filling the sky.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Gamma rays: The most energetic light there is; a gamma-ray burst from a dying star can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Photons: Photons are massless, so they can only move at light speed; light made in the Sun's core takes ages to escape, then just 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Infrared: William Herschel found it in 1800 when a thermometer placed just beyond red light's edge warmed up, revealing rays we feel as heat but cannot see.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Ultraviolet: Invisible to us, but bees and many birds see it, and some flowers carry UV patterns that act as landing strips.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Wi-Fi signals: It is just microwaves at about 2.4 or 5 GHz, so your router's signal moves at light speed; the 2.4 GHz band is shared with microwave ovens.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Sound: Sound needs air or another medium and crawls along at about 343 metres per second, roughly a million times slower than light; in vacuum it cannot travel at all.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Electrons: Electrons have mass, so none can ever reach light speed; particle accelerators push them to within a hair of it, but never all the way.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Neutrinos: Nearly massless, so they travel just under light speed; trillions pass harmlessly through your body every second.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Protons: The Large Hadron Collider drives protons to over 99.999999% of light speed, but anything with mass can never quite get there.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Cosmic rays: Mostly protons and atomic nuclei, so slower than light, though some are astonishingly close; the 1991 'Oh-My-God particle' hit with the energy of a thrown baseball.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Bullets: A rifle bullet is roughly three times the speed of sound, yet only a few millionths of light speed.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Space shuttle: It orbited at about 28,000 km/h, which sounds fast but is only around 0.003% of light speed.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Shock waves: They move faster than sound in the medium that creates them, but they are pressure fronts in matter, nowhere near light speed.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Tsunamis: In deep ocean a tsunami cruises at jetliner speed, around 800 km/h, which is still a tiny fraction of light speed.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Voyager 1: Launched in 1977 and now the farthest human-made object, it moves at about 17 km/s, yet its radio signals still take about a day to reach us.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Concorde: It cruised at about twice the speed of sound, around 2,150 km/h, which is still a tiny fraction of light speed.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Alpha particles: Helium nuclei thrown out by radioactive decay move at only a few percent of light speed, and a sheet of paper stops them.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Cheetah: The fastest land animal hits about 100 km/h, yet light could circle the Earth more than seven times in the second a sprint takes.
Travels at the speed of light (in a vacu.Meteors: They slam into the atmosphere at 11 to 72 km/s, fast enough to glow, but thousands of times slower than light.

Solo artists (not bands).Prince: Born Prince Rogers Nelson, named after his father's jazz trio. He later swapped his name for an unpronounceable symbol.

Solo artists (not bands).Elton John: Born Reginald Dwight, he took his stage name from bandmates Elton Dean and Long John Baldry.

Solo artists (not bands).Bob Dylan: Born Robert Zimmerman, he took his stage name partly from poet Dylan Thomas, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016.
Solo artists (not bands).Rihanna: From Barbados, she also built a billion-dollar business with Fenty Beauty and headlined the Super Bowl halftime show in 2023.
Solo artists (not bands).Shakira: Colombian star whose World Cup anthem Waka Waka has been watched billions of times on YouTube.
Solo artists (not bands).Ed Sheeran: He performs with a loop pedal, building layers of guitar and percussion live, all by himself.
Solo artists (not bands).Drake: The Toronto rapper started out as an actor on the teen drama Degrassi, before becoming one of streaming's biggest stars.
Solo artists (not bands).Bruno Mars: Born Peter Hernandez in Honolulu, he performed as a child Elvis impersonator, and even appeared in a 1992 film in that role.
Solo artists (not bands).Billie Eilish: In 2020, at 18, she became the youngest artist to win all four major Grammy categories in one night.
Solo artists (not bands).Pink Floyd: A band, named after bluesmen Pink Anderson and Floyd Council. Dark Side of the Moon stayed on the US chart for over 900 weeks.
Solo artists (not bands).Jethro Tull: A band, not a person: it's named after an 18th-century farming inventor. The frontman and flutist is Ian Anderson.

Solo artists (not bands).Blondie: A band, though many assume it's Debbie Harry's solo name. It came from catcalls she got on the street.
Solo artists (not bands).Franz Ferdinand: A Glasgow band named after the archduke whose 1914 assassination sparked World War I.
Solo artists (not bands).Steely Dan: A duo-led band, Walter Becker and Donald Fagen, named after a device in a William S. Burroughs novel.

Solo artists (not bands).Simply Red: A band despite being fronted by one man, Mick Hucknall. The name nods to his red hair.
Solo artists (not bands).The Killers: A band from Las Vegas, named after a fictional group in a New Order video, and not a solo artist, despite Brandon Flowers fronting it.

Jazz musicians.Louis Armstrong: Louis Armstrong, nicknamed Satchmo, was a trumpeter and singer; his 1967 What a Wonderful World is still beloved.
Jazz musicians.Miles Davis: His 1959 album Kind of Blue is often cited as the best-selling jazz album ever, and its cool modal sound reshaped the genre.
Jazz musicians.Duke Ellington: He led his orchestra for about half a century and wrote thousands of pieces, including Take the A Train's famous partner, Mood Indigo.
Jazz musicians.John Coltrane: His 1965 A Love Supreme is a spiritual landmark, and his rapid, dense soloing was nicknamed sheets of sound.
Jazz musicians.Charlie Parker: Nicknamed Bird, the saxophonist co-founded bebop in the 1940s with blazing speed and harmonic daring, and died aged 34.
Jazz musicians.Ella Fitzgerald: The First Lady of Song won 13 Grammys, and her scat singing was loved for pitch-perfect improvisation.
Jazz musicians.Billie Holiday: Lady Day recorded Strange Fruit in 1939, a harrowing protest song against lynching that was far ahead of its time.
Jazz musicians.Thelonious Monk: The pianist's angular, jolting style and his tune Round Midnight, one of the most recorded jazz standards, remain unmistakable.
Jazz musicians.Dizzy Gillespie: His trumpet's bell angled upward after a dancer fell on it, and he liked the sound so much he kept it.
Jazz musicians.Count Basie: The Kansas City bandleader's piano was famously sparse, a few notes with huge swing, driving one of the great big bands.
Jazz musicians.Herbie Hancock: He played in Miles Davis's band, then scored a 1983 hit, Rockit, with scratching turntables, bridging jazz and hip hop.
Jazz musicians.Benny Goodman: The King of Swing led a clarinet-fronted band, and his 1938 Carnegie Hall concert helped bring jazz into the concert hall.
Jazz musicians.Chet Baker: A trumpeter and singer with a delicate, breathy voice, his cool-jazz take on My Funny Valentine became his signature.
Jazz musicians.Elvis Presley: The King of Rock and Roll mixed country, gospel and blues, but he is not usually counted as a jazz musician.
Jazz musicians.Bob Marley: The reggae king from Jamaica, whose Exodus and One Love are global anthems, belongs to a different genre.
Jazz musicians.Johnny Cash: The Man in Black is a country and rock legend, famous for his Folsom Prison concert in 1968.
Jazz musicians.Jimi Hendrix: A trap for jazz fans: the rock guitarist admired Miles Davis and Coltrane, and loved to jam in jazzy ways, but isn't a jazz player.
Jazz musicians.Kurt Cobain: The Nirvana singer was a grunge icon, and his band's Unplugged set was acoustic, not jazz.
Jazz musicians.Dolly Parton: The Queen of Country wrote Jolene and I Will Always Love You, and her genre is country, not jazz.
Jazz musicians.Bob Dylan: The singer-songwriter won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016, and is a folk and rock poet, not a jazz star.
Jazz musicians.Freddie Mercury: Queen's flamboyant singer mixed rock, opera and funk, though the band's catalogue is rock, not jazz.
Jazz musicians.Madonna: The Queen of Pop reinvented herself endlessly, but her songs are pop and dance, not jazz.
Jazz musicians.Luciano Pavarotti: The Italian tenor was an opera star known for Nessun dorma, with a voice trained for the opera stage.
Jazz musicians.Mozart: The Austrian genius wrote music in the 1700s, long before jazz emerged in New Orleans around 1900.

Ice hockey terms.Puck: The puck is vulcanized rubber, 3 inches across and about 6 ounces, and it is frozen before games so it slides rather than bounces.
Ice hockey terms.Icing: Icing is called when a player shoots the puck from behind center ice past the opponent's goal line; it stops teams from just dumping it away.
Ice hockey terms.Power play: A power play gives one team a man advantage while the other serves a penalty, and a good one can score within seconds.
Ice hockey terms.Penalty box: Minor penalties send players to the box for two minutes, and the box is the only part of the rink where opposing players may sit side by side.
Ice hockey terms.Face-off: A face-off drops the puck between two centers, and the puck is dropped by the referee or linesman to restart play.
Ice hockey terms.Slap shot: A slap shot, made with a full wind-up, can send the puck over 160 km/h, and top players have been clocked past 175.
Ice hockey terms.Zamboni: Frank Zamboni, a California ice-rink owner, built his first resurfacing machine in 1949, and the name is now a trademark.
Ice hockey terms.Blue line: The blue lines mark the offensive zone, and offside is called if an attacker enters before the puck.
Ice hockey terms.Goalie: A goalie wears gear that can weigh more than 20 pounds, and the first masks were only worn in the 1950s and 60s after Jacques Plante.
Ice hockey terms.Body check: A body check is a legal hit with the hip or shoulder, though in women's hockey and youth leagues it is not allowed.
Ice hockey terms.Five-hole: The five-hole is the gap between a goalie's legs, and it got its name from the five spots a shooter may aim at.
Ice hockey terms.Wicket: A wicket is cricket's target; hockey nets measure 6 feet wide by 4 feet high and guard the goal.
Ice hockey terms.Bunt: A bunt is baseball's gentle tap; hockey's nearest thing is the soft dump-in, a puck sent deep for a chase.
Ice hockey terms.Touchdown: A touchdown is football's six-pointer; a hockey goal is worth a single point.
Ice hockey terms.Slam dunk: A slam dunk is basketball's, while hockey's showy score is the shootout move called a spin-o-rama.
Ice hockey terms.Love: Love is tennis for zero, and in hockey a shutout is the equivalent, a game without a goal against.
Ice hockey terms.Deuce: Deuce is tennis's 40-all, and hockey's tied games end with overtime and then a shootout.
Ice hockey terms.Scrum: A scrum is rugby's; in hockey, the pushing match in front of the net is called a scrum or scrap.
Ice hockey terms.Birdie: A birdie is golf's, but hockey's feathered fan favorite is the octopus thrown on the ice by Detroit Red Wings fans.
Ice hockey terms.Lineout: A lineout is rugby's throw-in; hockey has no throw-in because the boards keep the puck in play.
Ice hockey terms.Free throw: A free throw is basketball's; hockey's closest thing is the penalty shot, a one-on-one against the goalie.
Ice hockey terms.Strike: A strike is bowling's, and hockey's nearest thing is a hat trick, which fans mark by tossing their hats on the ice.
Ice hockey terms.Checkmate: Checkmate is chess; hockey's dramatic finish is sudden-death overtime, in which the first goal wins.
Ice hockey terms.Googly: A googly is cricket's; hockey's deceptive move is the deke, short for decoy.

Winter Olympic sports.Curling: Curling has been Olympic since the first Winter Games in 1924, and its stones are made of granite from Scotland's Ailsa Craig.
Winter Olympic sports.Biathlon: Biathlon blends cross-country skiing with rifle shooting, and misses at the range cost penalty laps or time.
Winter Olympic sports.Luge: Luge riders lie feet-first on their backs, steering with their calves and shoulders, at speeds that can top 140 km/h.
Winter Olympic sports.Skeleton: Skeleton riders go headfirst on a sled at up to about 130 km/h; it ran in 1928 and 1948 and returned for good in 2002.
Winter Olympic sports.Bobsleigh: Bobsleigh pairs and quads sprint to push the sled before jumping in, and the brakeman's job is to stop the sled after the finish.
Winter Olympic sports.Ice hockey: Ice hockey has been at the Winter Games since 1920, when it was actually part of the Summer Games, before the Winter Games existed.
Winter Olympic sports.Figure skating: Figure skating also began at the 1908 Summer Games, before the Winter Olympics began, and it's among the most-watched events.
Winter Olympic sports.Ski jumping: Ski jumpers sail beyond 100 meters on large hills, and women's ski jumping was only added to the Olympics in 2014.
Winter Olympic sports.Snowboarding: Snowboarding joined the Olympics in 1998 at Nagano and its halfpipe and big air events are crowd favorites.
Winter Olympic sports.Nordic combined: Nordic combined pairs a ski jump with a cross-country race, and the jump score decides each skier's head start in the race.
Winter Olympic sports.Speed skating: Speed skating has both long-track races, with pairs in lanes, and short-track, where packs jostle on a tight oval.
Winter Olympic sports.Alpine skiing: Alpine skiing covers downhill, slalom and giant slalom, and downhill racers can top 140 km/h.
Winter Olympic sports.Rowing: Rowing is a summer sport, and its Olympic debut was washed out: rough weather cancelled the 1896 races altogether.
Winter Olympic sports.Diving: Diving belongs to the summer Games, and the winter ones have no pool events.
Winter Olympic sports.Fencing: Fencing is a summer sport, and it's been in every modern Summer Games since 1896.
Winter Olympic sports.Archery: Archery is a summer sport; a winter cousin, the biathlon, swaps the bow for a rifle.
Winter Olympic sports.Triathlon: Triathlon is a summer sport with swim, bike and run, and it debuted at the Olympics in 2000.
Winter Olympic sports.Water polo: Water polo is a summer Olympic sport, and it was the first team sport at the Games, in 1900.
Winter Olympic sports.Handball: Handball is a summer sport; the indoor version with seven players a side joined in 1972, after a 1936 outdoor version.
Winter Olympic sports.Sailing: Sailing is a summer sport that dates back to 1900, and frozen water makes it unsuited to the Winter Games.
Winter Olympic sports.Cycling: Cycling is a summer sport, since track and road racing don't run on snow, though winter fat-bike races exist.
Winter Olympic sports.Bandy: Bandy has long been left out of the Winter Olympics despite its popularity in Russia and Scandinavia, and it was a demonstration sport in 1952.
Winter Olympic sports.Broomball: Broomball isn't an Olympic sport; it is played on ice in shoes, with a broom-like stick and a ball, and is popular in Canada.
Winter Olympic sports.Snowmobiling: Snowmobiling was never an Olympic sport; sled dog racing was a demonstration event at Lake Placid in 1932.

Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Sarajevo: The 1984 Games were the first in a socialist country, and the city's venues were badly damaged in the war.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Calgary: The 1988 Games had Jamaica's bobsled team debut, which inspired the film Cool Runnings.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Lillehammer: The 1994 Games in the Norwegian town were praised for their atmosphere and were held just two years after the previous Games.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Nagano: The 1998 Games included the first Olympic NHL players in hockey, and the Games were hosted in Japan.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Salt Lake City: The 2002 Games were held in Utah, and bidding scandals before it led to reforms in how the IOC picks hosts.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Aspen: The Colorado resort has hosted World Cup skiing events, but it has never hosted the Olympics.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Zermatt: The Swiss village below the Matterhorn is a famous ski resort that has never hosted the Winter Games.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Davos: Known for its World Economic Forum, the Swiss resort has never hosted the Olympics.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Vail: Colorado's ski resort has hosted alpine world championships, but not the Olympics.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Banff: The Canadian resort bid for the Games several times, but never got to host them.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Helsinki: The 1952 Summer Games were in the Finnish capital, so it's a Summer host and not a Winter one.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Athens: The birthplace of the Games is a Summer host, in 1896 and 2004, not a Winter one.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Sydney: It hosted the 2000 Summer Games, and Australia has never hosted a Winter Olympics.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Rio de Janeiro: The 2016 Summer Games were held here, and it was the first in South America.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Montreal: The 1976 Summer Games were held in the Quebec city, with a Winter Games never held there.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Seoul: The Summer Games of 1988 were here, though South Korea hosted the Winter Games in Pyeongchang in 2018.
Cities that have hosted the Winter Olymp.Barcelona: The Catalan city hosted the 1992 Summer Games, and no Winter Olympics has been held there.

Board games over a thousand years old.Chess: Chess arose in India around the 6th century as chaturanga and spread to Persia and Europe. The queen only became its strongest piece in the late 1400s.
Board games over a thousand years old.Go: Go has been played in China for roughly 2,500 years. Its board offers more possible positions than there are atoms in the observable universe.
Board games over a thousand years old.Mancala: Mancala is a family of sowing games played with seeds or stones in pits. Versions are found across Africa and Asia.
Board games over a thousand years old.Senet: Senet is an ancient Egyptian board game, found in tombs including Tutankhamun's. Its rules are only partly known.
Board games over a thousand years old.Backgammon: Backgammon descends from ancient Persian and Roman games, and is one of the oldest board games still played today.
Board games over a thousand years old.Royal Game of Ur: Found in graves at Ur in Mesopotamia and dated to about 2600 BCE. A cuneiform tablet from Babylon later preserved the rules.
Board games over a thousand years old.Nine men's morris: Boards for this strategy game are carved into medieval cathedral cloisters. Players form 'mills' of three in a row to remove opposing pieces.
Board games over a thousand years old.Hnefatafl: A Viking-era game with unequal sides: a king and defenders versus attackers twice as many. The king tries to reach the edge or corner.
Board games over a thousand years old.Pachisi: India's national game, played on a cross-shaped board with cowrie shells as dice. Ludo is a simplified descendant.
Board games over a thousand years old.Monopoly: Monopoly was patented in 1935 by Charles Darrow, but it came from The Landlord's Game, created by Elizabeth Magie in 1904 as a critique of landlords.
Board games over a thousand years old.Scrabble: Scrabble came out in 1948 from architect Alfred Butts, who figured out letter frequencies by counting letters in newspapers.
Board games over a thousand years old.Risk: Risk was invented by French filmmaker Albert Lamorisse in 1957, and he also made the film The Red Balloon.
Board games over a thousand years old.Catan: Catan debuted in Germany in 1995, helped to launch the modern board game boom; it was originally called The Settlers of Catan.
Board games over a thousand years old.Clue: Clue, known as Cluedo in the UK, was created in an English air-raid shelter during WWII era by a solicitor's clerk named Anthony Pratt.
Board games over a thousand years old.Stratego: Stratego is a Dutch game dating from around 1946, and its roots go back to a French game called L'Attaque.
Board games over a thousand years old.Othello: Othello's modern form came from 1970s Japan, though its roots lie in Reversi from the 1880s; it takes a minute to learn.
Board games over a thousand years old.Battleship: Battleship started as a pencil-and-paper game played by soldiers in WWI, long before the plastic version in the 1960s.
Board games over a thousand years old.Connect Four: Connect Four was released in 1974, and computers have solved it: with perfect play, the first player always wins.
Board games over a thousand years old.Trivial Pursuit: Trivial Pursuit was devised in 1979 by two Canadian journalists in a few hours, and it sold millions in the 1980s.
Board games over a thousand years old.Mastermind: Invented in 1970 by Mordecai Meirowitz, an Israeli postmaster, as a code-breaking game based on an older pencil game.
Board games over a thousand years old.Ticket to Ride: Alan Moon's 2004 train game has you claim railway routes across a map. It's one of the best-known modern hobby games.
Board games over a thousand years old.Candy Land: Candy Land was created in 1948 by Eleanor Abbott while recovering from polio, to entertain children in a hospital ward.
Board games over a thousand years old.Sorry!: Sorry! dates to 1929 in Britain and is based on the older game Parcheesi, though it's far younger than a thousand years.
Board games over a thousand years old.Pictionary: Pictionary was invented in 1985 by Rob Angel, a waiter in Seattle, and has sold tens of millions of copies. It's only a few decades old.

From the legend of Robin Hood.Sherwood Forest: The Nottinghamshire woodland of the ballads is real, and its Major Oak is said to be 800 to 1,000 years old.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Little John: Robin's right-hand man; ballads say he was named ironically, since he was a giant of a man.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Maid Marian: She was not in the earliest ballads; she joined the legend through later May Day plays and became Robin's love.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Friar Tuck: The fighting friar who is Robin's cheerful, well-fed companion, often shown as a drinker with a quarterstaff.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Nottingham: Robin's enemy the Sheriff held office in this real English city, which today still has a Robin Hood statue by its castle.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Will Scarlet: One of the Merry Men, whose name varies as Scarlock or Scadlock in older ballads, and who has a hot temper.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Longbow: Robin's weapon; English longbowmen could loose around ten arrows a minute and won battles at Crecy and Agincourt.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Prince John: Richard the Lionheart's scheming brother, who really did rule in his absence and later became King John, signing Magna Carta in 1215.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Much the Miller: One of Robin's earliest outlaws, called the miller's son in the oldest ballads.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Alan-a-Dale: The minstrel of the band, who gets help from Robin to marry his true love instead of an old knight.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Excalibur: A trap: Arthur's sword belongs to a different legend, set in mythic Britain, not Sherwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Merlin: A trap: Arthur's wizard belongs to Camelot; Robin's legend is gritty and has no sorcery in it.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Camelot: A trap: Arthur's court belongs to a legendary Britain of knights and magic; Robin's stronghold is the greenwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Lancelot: A trap: Camelot's greatest knight is Arthurian; Robin's tales have nothing like his romance with Guinevere.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Guinevere: A trap: Arthur's queen belongs to Camelot, not to Sherwood, where Robin's love is Marian.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Holy Grail: A trap: the Grail quest belongs to Arthur's knights, while Robin's band chases tax money and a corrupt sheriff.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Mordred: A trap: Arthur's treacherous nephew belongs to Camelot's fall, not to Nottingham's greenwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Avalon: A trap: the misty isle where Arthur was carried belongs to Camelot's legend, never to Sherwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Don Quixote: A trap: Cervantes's 1605 Spanish knight-errant is a satire of chivalry, far from Sherwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.William Tell: A Swiss legendary archer, the one forced to shoot an apple from his son's head; a trap, as he's another famous archer.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Beowulf: A trap: this Old English epic hero is Scandinavian by setting, and nothing to do with Sherwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Galahad: A trap: the pure Grail knight is Arthurian, and has no place among Robin's outlaws in the greenwood.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Lady of the Lake: A trap: the water spirit who handed Arthur his sword belongs to Camelot's stories, not Robin's.
From the legend of Robin Hood.Round Table: A trap: Arthur's equality-minded table belongs to Camelot, not to Robin's greenwood.

Historic coins no longer in use.Denarius: Rome's silver workhorse for centuries. Its name lives on in the 'd' of old British pence and in the Arabic and Balkan dinar.
Historic coins no longer in use.Sestertius: A big Roman brass coin worth a quarter of a denarius. Its wide face let emperors show off portraits and building projects.
Historic coins no longer in use.Doubloon: A Spanish gold coin worth two escudos, hence the name 'double'. Pirate stories made it famous, though few pirates ever saw many.
Historic coins no longer in use.Piece of eight: The Spanish silver peso, split into eight reales. It was trusted worldwide and became the model for the US dollar.
Historic coins no longer in use.Ducat: Venice minted this gold coin from 1284 and kept its purity for centuries, making it a trade standard across Europe.
Historic coins no longer in use.Farthing: Britain's quarter-penny, last struck in 1956 and withdrawn in 1960. A tiny wren was shown on its back.
Historic coins no longer in use.Groat: An English silver fourpenny coin introduced under Edward I. Saying someone 'isn't worth a groat' meant they were worthless.
Historic coins no longer in use.Obol: A small ancient Greek silver coin. Tradition says the dead were buried with one to pay Charon, the ferryman of the underworld.
Historic coins no longer in use.Aureus: Roman gold coin worth 25 silver denarii. It was so valuable that a single one could cover a legionary's pay for months.
Historic coins no longer in use.Solidus: Constantine introduced this gold coin in the 300s. It stayed reliable for centuries and gave us the word 'soldier', one who is paid.
Historic coins no longer in use.Drachma: Greece's money for millennia until the euro arrived in 2002. The name means 'handful', since it equalled six obol spits.
Historic coins no longer in use.Half crown: A British coin worth two shillings and sixpence. It disappeared around decimalisation in 1970 along with its fractions.
Historic coins no longer in use.Euro: Trap: very much in use. About twenty countries have used it since 2002, so it isn't a retired coin.
Historic coins no longer in use.Bitcoin: Trap: a digital currency from 2009 that is still traded daily. It was never a historic physical coin either.
Historic coins no longer in use.Yen: Trap: Japan's current currency since 1871. The name simply means 'round object', after the shape of its coins.
Historic coins no longer in use.Rupee: Trap: still the money of India, Pakistan, Nepal and others. The name comes from Sanskrit for silver.
Historic coins no longer in use.Yuan: Trap: China's current currency. Yuan also means 'round', like the yen, from the coin shape.
Historic coins no longer in use.Won: Trap: the active currency of both Koreas. It descends from the same root as the yuan and yen, meaning 'round'.
Historic coins no longer in use.Rand: Trap: South Africa's money today, named after the Witwatersrand ridge, where the gold rush began in 1886.
Historic coins no longer in use.Krona: Trap: Sweden's current currency, plus Iceland's. 'Krona' means crown, as does Denmark's krone.
Historic coins no longer in use.Baht: Trap: Thailand's current currency. It began as a unit of weight for silver, so the name is far older than its notes.
Historic coins no longer in use.Naira: Trap: Nigeria's money since 1973, when it replaced the Nigerian pound. Still circulating, so not historic.
Historic coins no longer in use.Riyal: Trap: used in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and elsewhere. Its name echoes the Spanish 'real', so it has Iberian roots.
Historic coins no longer in use.Rupiah: Trap: Indonesia's current currency. Its name comes from the rupee, brought by traders from India.

Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Metal spoon: Metal on spinning blades can chip the blade, scratch the jug and send shards into your smoothie, and it may jam the motor outright.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Fork: A fork wedges between the blades and the jar, and the resulting screech is the sound of both being ruined.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Smartphone: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and crushing one can spark a fire, which is why blending a phone is a stunt performed with serious safety gear.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Pebbles: Stones are harder than most blender blades, so they dull the edges and can crack the jar, and hot fragments may fly.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Car keys: Besides ruining the blade, the key's metal and plastic fob would be ground into slivers that no one wants in a drink.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Chopsticks: Wood or bamboo splinters under blade force, and the fibers could jam the blades while sending sharp bits through your drink.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Lego bricks: The plastic is tough ABS, famously durable; a Lego brick can survive years of play, and a blender would only shred it into sharp bits.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Tennis ball: The felt, rubber and pressurized air make this a mess: it bounces around, stalls the blades and might burst out of the jar.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Socks: Fabric wraps around the blade shaft and binds the motor, a classic way to burn out a blender in seconds.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Coins: Metal coins damage the blades and the jar, and they can shed copper or nickel bits, which makes this a very expensive smoothie.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Batteries: Cutting a battery can leak toxic chemicals or ignite it, so this is among the most dangerous things a blender could be asked to chop.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Paper clips: Thin steel bends and snags on the blades, and the sharp fragments are hard to spot in food.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Banana: Bananas are a smoothie classic, and a frozen sliced banana gives a creamy, ice-cream like texture without any dairy.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Strawberries: A strawberry is not a true berry, botanically speaking, and the seeds on the outside are each a separate fruit.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Spinach: Spinach blends into smoothies nearly tasteless, and its supposed iron boost was inflated by a decimal point error, a famously retold myth.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Milk: Blending milk too long makes foam, because the air whipped in is stabilized by milk proteins, which is also how cappuccino froth works.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Yogurt: Yogurt adds creaminess and live cultures, and its tang comes from bacteria turning milk sugar into lactic acid.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Ice cubes: Blenders are designed to crush ice; the trick is to add liquid first so the blades have something to pull ice through.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Mango: Mangoes are related to cashews and poison ivy, and the skin has a compound that can give sensitive people a rash.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Oats: Blending oats into flour is a handy kitchen trick, and a blender can make oat flour in under a minute.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Peanut butter: Thick peanut butter blends fine in a smoothie, and a powerful blender can turn roasted peanuts into butter in minutes.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Orange juice: Blending the whole peeled fruit differs from juicing, as it keeps the fiber, and in the blender the white pith adds bitterness.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Blueberries: Their dusty bloom is a natural wax that protects the fruit, and blueberries blend into a smoothie with a vivid purple color.
Things you shouldn't put in a blender.Honey: Honey never spoils in sealed jars, and archaeologists have reported edible honey in ancient Egyptian tombs.

Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Cast iron skillet: Detergent strips the baked-on oil layer called seasoning, leaving bare iron that rusts, so a skillet is wiped, not washed with soap, by tradition.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Wooden cutting board: Heat and soaking make wood swell, warp and crack, and the splits then hide bacteria, so boards are hand washed and oiled.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Smartphone: Even water resistant phones are rated for fresh water at limited depth, and dishwasher heat and detergent can wreck the seals.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Laptop: Beyond water, detergent and heat would cook the circuits and battery, a wash that no machine would survive.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Teddy bear: Machine washing is usually fine for bears, but a dishwasher's heat and harsh detergents would melt glue and mat the fur.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Wooden spoon: Hot water dries out the grain, making the spoon rough and cracked, and splinters could end up in the pot.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Electric kettle: The base holds electrical parts, and a dishwasher is a very quick way to destroy it, never mind the shock hazard.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Toaster: Crumbs are not the problem here; water would ruin the heating elements and wiring, and could leave it unsafe to use.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Wristwatch: Water resistance ratings assume still, cool water, so hot jets and detergent can degrade the gaskets and ruin the movement.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Library book: Paper pages would swell and turn to pulp, and the librarian would have much to say about the fine.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Hair dryer: Water inside the motor and heating coil is a recipe for a short circuit, and a wet dryer can be a shock risk.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Cat: Cats are famously not fans of baths, and a dishwasher's heat and noise would make this about as unsafe as it sounds.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Dinner plate: The dishwasher exists for these; it was invented by Josephine Cochrane in 1886 because servants kept chipping her china.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Drinking glass: Glasses go in, but repeated hot cycles can etch them with a permanent cloudy film, especially in hard water.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Cereal bowl: Ceramic bowls usually take the heat in stride, and most are labeled dishwasher safe.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Fork: Stainless steel handles detergent well, and forks are also dishwasher regulars as long as they are not silver plated or antique.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Teaspoon: Teaspoons ride along happily in the cutlery basket, though stacked spoons can nest together and stay unwashed.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Ceramic mug: A glazed ceramic mug is built to survive a hot wash, though old hand-painted ones may fade.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Glass mixing bowl: Tempered glass handles the dishwasher's heat comfortably, which is why mixing bowls are usually sturdy enough for it.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Saucer: It is flat, ceramic and stable, so it gets cleaned perfectly well on the rack.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Soup bowl: A deep bowl needs to face down so water can drain, but is otherwise about as dishwasher friendly as dishes get.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Steel saucepan: Stainless steel pans clean up nicely in the dishwasher, unlike the aluminum kind, which can darken.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Butter knife: Blunt, simple and stainless, a butter knife handles the cycle fine, unlike a sharp chef's knife, which dulls.
Things you shouldn't put in a dishwasher.Ramekin: Ceramic ramekins are baked in kilns well beyond any dishwasher temperature, so they take the cycle without complaint.

Parts of the hand.Palm: The palm has dense nerve endings and, uniquely, ridges like fingertips, which give every hand its own print.
Parts of the hand.Thumb: The thumb is opposable, so it can touch each finger, and this grip is one reason humans can use tools.
Parts of the hand.Knuckle: A knuckle is a finger joint, and the cracking noise comes from gas bubbles in the joint fluid.
Parts of the hand.Fingernail: Fingernails are made of keratin, the same stuff as hair, and they grow about three millimeters per month.
Parts of the hand.Fingertip: Fingertips have some of the densest touch receptors on the body, and they can feel details smaller than a hair's width.
Parts of the hand.Pinky: The pinky has the fewest muscle fibers of the fingers but still gives about half of your grip strength.
Parts of the hand.Index finger: The index finger is the pointing finger. It has its own extra muscle, so you can point alone.
Parts of the hand.Ring finger: The ring finger is named for wedding rings, thought by the ancient Romans to have a vein leading directly to the heart.
Parts of the hand.Metacarpal: Metacarpals are the five bones in the palm, linking wrist bones to the fingers.
Parts of the hand.Middle finger: The middle finger is usually the longest of the five.
Parts of the hand.Heel: The heel is part of the foot, and it carries your weight first when you walk.
Parts of the hand.Arch: The arch of the foot acts like a spring, and its shape stores energy as you step.
Parts of the hand.Sole: The sole is the underside of the foot, and it has about 200,000 nerve endings.
Parts of the hand.Big toe: The big toe is on the foot, and it takes much of your weight when you push off.
Parts of the hand.Instep: The instep is the arched part of the foot between toes and ankle.
Parts of the hand.Ankle: The ankle joins foot to leg, so it isn't part of the hand.
Parts of the hand.Toenail: Toenails are on the foot. They grow much slower than fingernails.
Parts of the hand.Elbow: The elbow is part of the arm, so it's not in the hand.
Parts of the hand.Forearm: The forearm sits between elbow and wrist, so it's not part of the hand.
Parts of the hand.Shin: The shin is the front of the lower leg, so it's not part of the hand.
Parts of the hand.Bunion: A bunion is a bony bump at the base of the big toe, so it belongs to the foot.
Parts of the hand.Achilles tendon: The Achilles tendon links the calf to the heel, and it's in the leg.
Parts of the hand.Kneecap: The kneecap is part of the knee, not the hand.
Parts of the hand.Calf: The calf is the back of the lower leg, so it's not part of the hand.

Things made of keratin.Hair: Hair is dead keratin pushed out by living follicles, and a single strand can hold up to about 100 grams before breaking.
Things made of keratin.Fingernails: Fingernails grow around 3 millimeters a month, roughly four times faster than toenails, and grow faster on your dominant hand.
Things made of keratin.Toenails: A toenail takes about a year to grow out fully, much slower than a fingernail, because less blood reaches your feet.
Things made of keratin.Hooves: A horse's hoof is hardened keratin much like your fingernail, which is why farriers can trim and shoe it painlessly.
Things made of keratin.Feathers: Feather keratin is a tough beta-keratin that lets birds' feathers be both light and strong enough for flight.
Things made of keratin.Claws: Claws are keratin sheaths over bone, and cats can retract theirs to keep them sharp for hunting.
Things made of keratin.Rhino horn: Rhino horn has no bone and is just compacted keratin, the same stuff as fingernails, which makes the poaching trade especially tragic.
Things made of keratin.Wool: Wool is keratin spun from sheep, and its natural crimp traps air, making it insulate even when damp.
Things made of keratin.Porcupine quills: Quills are modified hairs made of keratin, and some bear tiny backward-pointing barbs that make them hard to pull out.
Things made of keratin.Baleen: Whales like humpbacks strain krill through baleen plates made of keratin instead of having teeth.
Things made of keratin.Hedgehog spines: A hedgehog carries around 5,000 to 7,000 spines, which are hollow, keratin-based hairs that cushion falls.
Things made of keratin.Teeth: A trap: teeth are mostly mineral. Enamel, the hardest substance in the body, is not keratin.
Things made of keratin.Bone: Bone is built of collagen and calcium phosphate, not keratin, and it is living tissue that constantly rebuilds itself.
Things made of keratin.Cartilage: Cartilage is made of collagen, not keratin. Your ears and nose tip are bendy because of it.
Things made of keratin.Antlers: Antlers are true bone, regrown every year, unlike horns, which are keratin over a bone core.
Things made of keratin.Ivory: Ivory is dentine, a tooth material, so elephant tusks are overgrown teeth rather than keratin.
Things made of keratin.Pearls: Pearls are layers of nacre, made of calcium carbonate that a mollusk coats around an irritant.
Things made of keratin.Seashells: Shells are calcium carbonate secreted by the animal's mantle, so they are mineral rather than keratin.
Things made of keratin.Coral: Coral skeletons are limestone secreted by tiny polyps, which are animals, not the plants many people assume.
Things made of keratin.Silk: Silk is a protein, but fibroin from silkworm cocoons rather than keratin, and one cocoon can be a single thread over 900 meters long.
Things made of keratin.Cotton: Cotton is plant cellulose, so unlike wool it has no keratin at all.
Things made of keratin.Enamel: Tooth enamel is about 96 percent mineral, making it harder than bone, yet it contains no living cells and can't regrow.
Things made of keratin.Eggshell: Eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate, riddled with thousands of tiny pores that let the embryo breathe.
Things made of keratin.Spider web: Spider silk is a different protein than keratin, and by weight it's stronger than steel.

Classic magician props.Top hat: Magicians use top hats because a hollow crown is a hiding place, a trick popularized in the 19th century.
Classic magician props.Magic wand: A wand often doubles as misdirection: the audience's eyes follow it while the other hand does the secret work.
Classic magician props.White rabbit: The rabbit-from-a-hat trick is a stage classic from the 1800s, and many magicians now use plush ones to spare animals.
Classic magician props.Deck of cards: A standard deck has 52 cards, and the number of possible shuffles is vastly larger than the number of atoms on Earth.
Classic magician props.Silk scarves: Silk scarves are favorites since they pack tiny and expand, and they're light enough to hide in a palm.
Classic magician props.Cape: A cape provides cover for secret moves, and its dramatic flourish pulls attention away.
Classic magician props.Linking rings: The linking rings seem to pass through each other, but the secret is one ring that has a gap.
Classic magician props.Dove: Doves are small and calm, and magician Channing Pollock was famous for producing them.
Classic magician props.Cups and balls: The cups and balls trick is among the oldest in magic, and it's been performed for roughly two thousand years or more.
