Classic magician props.Stethoscope: Rene Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816 using a rolled paper tube, and doctors use it to hear body sounds.
Classic magician props.Lawnmower: The lawnmower was invented by Edwin Budding, who got the idea from a cloth-trimming machine in a textile mill.
Classic magician props.Spatula: Spatulas flip and spread food, and the word comes from the Latin for a flat blade.
Classic magician props.Hard hat: Hard hats were invented by Edward Bullard in 1919 and are made for safety.
Classic magician props.Paintbrush: A paintbrush paints a picture, rather than conjuring one out of thin air.
Classic magician props.Microscope: Microscopes magnify tiny things, and Dutch lens grinder Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria.
Classic magician props.Tuba: The tuba is the biggest brass instrument, with tubing that can stretch over five meters when uncoiled.
Classic magician props.Scuba tank: Scuba tanks hold compressed air, not pure oxygen, and scuba stands for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus.
Classic magician props.Toilet plunger: A toilet plunger works by pushing and pulling water, not magic, and it's strictly a plumber's tool.
Classic magician props.Tractor: A tractor is a farm vehicle, though David Copperfield did make something as big as the Statue of Liberty vanish in 1983.
Classic magician props.Rolling pin: Rolling pins are kitchen tools, though in comics they're a famous weapon of angry wives.
Classic magician props.Bicycle pump: A bicycle pump inflates tires, and the pneumatic tire was invented by John Boyd Dunlop in 1888.
Classic magician props.Garden hose: The first flexible firefighting hoses were made of sewn leather in the 1600s.
Classic magician props.Calculator: Pocket calculators arrived in the 1970s, and magicians do mental-math tricks with no device.
Classic magician props.Stapler: Staplers reportedly date to 18th-century France, where one was made for King Louis XV with each staple bearing a royal emblem.

Things that don't belong on a pizza.Toothpaste: Toothpaste on pizza sounds odd, and it's a famously fierce prank topping since mint clashes hard with cheese and tomato.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Shampoo: Shampoo would turn a pizza into a soapy mess, and it's a tongue-in-cheek no-go compared with the real toppings we love.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Crayons: Crayons are made of wax and pigment, and they'd melt in a hot oven into a colorful, greasy pool on the crust.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Socks: Socks would scorch fast, since wood-fired pizza ovens run around 430 C and cook a Neapolitan pie in about 90 seconds.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Glitter: Glitter looks festive but is plastic or mica, so edible-glitter makers use sugar and starch to make it safe to eat.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Gravel: Gravel would crack teeth, and the only stone near a pizza is the baking stone beneath it, which gives the crust its crunch.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Soap: Soap is the classic 'no' food, and a century ago some folks cooked with lard-based fats very close to soap-making ingredients.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Sand: Sand has been used to bake: some traditional Bedouin cooks bury dough in hot sand to make bread, but it's never a topping.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Bubble gum: Bubble gum stays chewy because its gum base is synthetic rubber, so it would never melt into cheese like a proper topping.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Rubber bands: Rubber bands would melt in a hot oven and smell terrible, and cooks only use them to tie meat for roasting.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Paper clips: Paper clips are metal and would cook into the cheese, a hard no for pizza even though real toppings are plenty.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Shoe polish: Shoe polish is a wax and solvent mixture that is toxic to eat, unlike a pizza's well-loved real sauces and cheeses.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Pepperoni: A trap: pepperoni is an American invention, not Italian, and in Italy 'peperoni' just means bell peppers.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Mushrooms: Mushrooms are among the top pizza toppings, and they release water as they cook, which is why many cooks pre-sauté them.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Olives: Olives have topped Mediterranean flatbreads for centuries, and black and green ones are the same fruit at different ripeness.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Basil: Basil is the herb on the classic Margherita, along with the red tomato and white mozzarella that mirror Italy's flag.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Mozzarella: Real mozzarella di bufala comes from water buffalo milk near Naples, and it's the traditional cheese for Neapolitan pizza.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Onions: Onions add sweetness when baked, and their sulfur compounds are why they make you cry when you slice them.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Ham: Ham and pineapple is the divisive Hawaiian pizza, and it was invented in Canada in the 1960s, not Hawaii.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Sausage: Sausage is a hearty pizza topping, and Italian-American pizzerias often crumble fennel-flavored pork sausage on top.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Peppers: Bell peppers are a popular pizza topping, and they go from green to red as they ripen, getting sweeter along the way.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Spinach: Spinach is a lighter pizza topping, and in the old cartoons Popeye made it famous as a strength food.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Anchovies: Anchovies are a polarizing pizza topping, and they're salty, cured fish that melt into the sauce, adding savory depth.
Things that don't belong on a pizza.Tomato sauce: Tomato sauce wasn't on pizza until the 1700s, since tomatoes arrived from the Americas and were first viewed with suspicion.

Things that melt in a hot car.Ice cream: Ice cream starts melting around -2 C, so on a hot day in a closed car, a tub turns into soup in minutes.
Things that melt in a hot car.Chocolate bar: Chocolate melts at around body temperature, which is why it feels so good in your mouth, and why it goes soft in a hot car.
Things that melt in a hot car.Crayons: Crayons are mostly paraffin wax, which softens at under 60 C, and car interiors can easily exceed that in summer sun.
Things that melt in a hot car.Popsicle: Popsicles turn into sticky syrup because they're mostly sugar water; a closed car can reach over 60 C in summer.
Things that melt in a hot car.Butter: Butter softens at around 30 C, and a hot car can easily get beyond that, turning it into liquid.
Things that melt in a hot car.Candle: Candle wax begins to soften from about 50 C, and many a candle has been found bent in a summer car.
Things that melt in a hot car.Lip balm: Lip balm is mostly wax and oil, so it can melt into a pool in a hot car, which also may spoil its smell.
Things that melt in a hot car.Snowball: A snowball in a hot car melts quickly, since the cabin can be 20 C or more hotter than outside within an hour.
Things that melt in a hot car.Ice cube: Cars act like greenhouses, trapping sunlight so interior temperatures can climb 20 C above the outside within an hour.
Things that melt in a hot car.Snow cone: Snow cones are mostly shaved ice, so they melt in minutes; it's also why they're eaten quickly on warm days.
Things that melt in a hot car.Book: Books survive heat, though a baking dashboard can warp covers; the paper is fine well past car temperatures.
Things that melt in a hot car.Shoe: Rubber and leather soles won't melt in a hot car, though the glue holding them can weaken and a sole may peel.
Things that melt in a hot car.Umbrella: Fabric and metal ribs shrug off car heat; the umbrella may get hot, but nothing in it melts at a car's temperature.
Things that melt in a hot car.Road map: Paper doesn't melt, and ignites only near 230 C, far above anything a parked car reaches, so a map survives.
Things that melt in a hot car.Coins: Coins are metal, which melts at hundreds of degrees; a dashboard coin can burn your fingers but stays solid.
Things that melt in a hot car.Keys: Keys won't melt, but metal in a sunny car gets hot enough to burn skin; seat belt buckles are notorious for it.
Things that melt in a hot car.Pencil: A pencil's graphite doesn't melt below about 3,600 C, and the wood survives, so it's a safe item to leave.
Things that melt in a hot car.Pillow: A pillow's fibres soften only at far higher temperatures, so it just gets warm and stuffy in a hot car.
Things that melt in a hot car.Carrot: A carrot won't melt, but it will go limp as it loses water; a heated car can reach 60 C, enough to wilt veg.
Things that melt in a hot car.Teddy bear: Stuffed toys won't melt, but plastic pellets inside and glued eyes can warp, and the car's heat can make them smell.
Things that melt in a hot car.Jacket: Polyester only melts at around 250 C, far above car temperature, so a jacket gets hot but stays intact.
Things that melt in a hot car.Apple: An apple won't melt; it will soften and ferment in a baking car, and can even become mushy within hours.
Things that melt in a hot car.Baseball cap: A cap is fabric with a plastic brim stiffener that can warp, but it won't melt in car heat.
Things that melt in a hot car.Tennis racket: A tennis racket won't melt, but heat can loosen string tension and weaken glue, which is why players don't leave one in the car.

Clergy and religious roles.Priest: In Catholic tradition a priest can't marry once ordained, yet the Eastern Catholic churches have long ordained married men.
Clergy and religious roles.Bishop: The word bishop comes from Greek episkopos, meaning overseer, and a bishop's pointed hat, the mitre, is said to echo a flame of Pentecost.
Clergy and religious roles.Rabbi: Rabbi means my teacher in Hebrew, and rabbis are not priests: they are scholars and teachers, not intermediaries who perform sacrifices.
Clergy and religious roles.Imam: Imam means one who stands in front, the person who leads prayer. In Sunni Islam any knowledgeable Muslim may lead, no ordination required.
Clergy and religious roles.Vicar: The word means a stand-in: a vicar once acted on behalf of a parish's rector, who collected the church's income.
Clergy and religious roles.Pastor: Pastor is Latin for shepherd, so a congregation is literally a flock, and the image runs through Christian teaching.
Clergy and religious roles.Deacon: Deacons are the oldest order of church helpers, with roots in the book of Acts, where seven were chosen to serve food to widows.
Clergy and religious roles.Monk: Benedictine monks follow a rule written around 530 AD that is still used, and monastery scribes preserved much ancient writing.
Clergy and religious roles.Nun: Many nuns lived in cloistered communities for centuries, and medieval convents were also centers of medicine, learning and book copying.
Clergy and religious roles.Cardinal: Cardinals are named for the Latin cardo, a hinge, and the red they wear is a sign of readiness to shed blood for the faith.
Clergy and religious roles.Pope: Pope comes from the Greek for father. The Vatican, where he lives, is the smallest independent state in the world.
Clergy and religious roles.Chaplain: The word chaplain comes from the cappella, the cloak of St. Martin of Tours, kept as a relic in a small chapel.
Clergy and religious roles.Archbishop: An archbishop leads a province of several bishops, and the Archbishop of Canterbury is the senior bishop of the Church of England.
Clergy and religious roles.Senator: Senator comes from Latin senex, old man: the Roman Senate was a council of elders, not clergy, so this is politics, not religion.
Clergy and religious roles.Mayor: A mayor runs a city. The word comes from Latin maior, greater, and it is a secular office, not a religious role.
Clergy and religious roles.Judge: A judge decides cases in court, a legal not religious role, though the biblical Book of Judges describes leaders who were both.
Clergy and religious roles.Sheriff: The word comes from Old English shire-reeve, the king's officer of a county, which makes it a law-enforcement title, not a clergy one.
Clergy and religious roles.Prime Minister: Britain's first prime minister is usually said to be Robert Walpole in the 1720s, a political, not church, office.
Clergy and religious roles.Governor: Governors run states or colonies. It comes from the Latin gubernare, to steer, the same root as the word for a ship's steering.
Clergy and religious roles.Chancellor: Chancellor began as a church scribe or secretary who worked behind a latticed screen, called cancelli, which is why the trap is tempting.
Clergy and religious roles.Squire: A squire was a knight's apprentice or a rural landowner, a feudal rank rather than a religious one.
Clergy and religious roles.Baron: Baron is the lowest rank of nobility in the British peerage, a feudal rank rather than a church one, though bishops also sit among lords.
Clergy and religious roles.Duke: A duke is the highest rank of British nobility below royalty, from Latin dux, leader, a title of rank not religion.
Clergy and religious roles.Earl: Earl is the one British noble title with no feminine form and no foreign equivalent: an earl's wife is a countess.

Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Blood pressure: The two numbers are pressure as the heart beats and as it rests, in mmHg, a unit inherited from old mercury columns.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Pulse: A resting adult pulse of 60 to 100 beats a minute is typical, while very fit athletes can sit well below 60.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Temperature: The famous 37 degrees C norm dates to the 1800s; modern studies find the average is a bit lower and drifts through the day.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Weight: Your weight can swing a kilo or more in a day through food, water and sweat, so clinics care more about trends.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Height: You are about a centimetre or two taller in the morning, because gravity slowly squashes the discs in your spine all day.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Cholesterol: Your liver makes most of your cholesterol itself; the body needs it for cell walls and hormones, so only excess is a problem.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Blood sugar: Fasting glucose is checked because persistently high levels point to diabetes; healthy bodies hold it in a narrow band using insulin.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.BMI: Devised in the 1830s by Belgian statistician Adolphe Quetelet to describe populations, which is why it misjudges muscular individuals.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Oxygen level: A fingertip clip reads it with red and infrared light; healthy readings are usually 95 percent or higher.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Inseam: A tailor's measure, from crotch to ankle. Trouser labels like 32 by 34 pair it with waist size; doctors don't care.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Collar size: Shirt makers use neck circumference for it. A doctor may note neck size only when screening for sleep apnea, so it's a near miss.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.IQ: Psychologists test it, not a routine checkup; the scale is built so the average score is set at 100.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Shoe size: A fitter's number, and national scales disagree: UK, US and EU sizes all differ, so a doctor can't use it.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Credit score: It tracks borrowing history, not health; the common US FICO scale runs from 300 to 850.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Hat size: A hatter's head-circumference number. Doctors do measure head size, but only on babies, as a growth check.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Ring size: Jewellers measure it, though doctors sometimes ask you to remove rings because a swollen finger can trap one.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Horsepower: James Watt coined it in the 1700s to sell steam engines by comparing them to draft horses; it rates engines, not patients.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Wind speed: Weather stations measure it with an anemometer; the Beaufort scale of 1805 grades it by its effects on sails and trees.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Shirt size: Clothing sizes belong to the tailor; the doctor weighs and measures you but never asks whether you're a medium.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Typing speed: Counted in words per minute, where a word is conventionally five characters; skilled typists often top 60.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Golf handicap: It rates a golfer against par; the best amateurs have a handicap near zero, and 'plus' handicaps go below it.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Bank balance: The one number a checkup doesn't record, though the bill afterwards might change it.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Screen time: Phones track it, and a doctor may ask about it, but it isn't a measurement taken at the checkup.
Things measured at a doctor's checkup.Rent: A payment for use of property, not a body measure; the word comes from Old French rente, meaning income.

Things a fishmonger sells.Salmon: Salmon return from the sea to the very river where they hatched, finding it by smell, sometimes after traveling thousands of kilometers.
Things a fishmonger sells.Cod: Cod was so important to Massachusetts that a wooden "Sacred Cod" has hung in the State House since the 1700s.
Things a fishmonger sells.Tuna: Bluefin tuna can warm their blood and swim at highway speeds, and a single prized fish has sold for over a million dollars in Tokyo.
Things a fishmonger sells.Prawns: In Britain, prawn and shrimp are used loosely, but prawns are a distinct group with branching gills, unlike shrimps.
Things a fishmonger sells.Mussels: Mussels anchor to rocks with strong threads called byssus, which people once spun into a fine, golden cloth.
Things a fishmonger sells.Oysters: Oysters can switch sex during their lives, and a single one filters tens of liters of water a day.
Things a fishmonger sells.Haddock: Haddock is famous in smoked form, and a dark mark behind its head is said in legend to be the thumbprint of Saint Peter.
Things a fishmonger sells.Mackerel: Mackerel are rich in omega-3 oils and spoil quickly, which is why they have always been sold fresh and fast.
Things a fishmonger sells.Crab: The "crab" shape evolves again and again in nature, a process called carcinization, and many are not true crabs.
Things a fishmonger sells.Lobster: Lobsters were once so common they were fed to prisoners and servants, and some people were embarrassed to be seen eating them.
Things a fishmonger sells.Squid: A squid has three hearts and blue blood, and some species can change color in a flash to signal or hide.
Things a fishmonger sells.Sardines: Sardines are named after the island of Sardinia, and huge shoals of them migrate along South Africa's coast each year.
Things a fishmonger sells.Sausages: They belong at a butcher's, since sausage-making uses minced meat and casings, not a thing from the sea.
Things a fishmonger sells.Bacon: Bacon is cured pork, and sold at the butcher; the old phrase "bring home the bacon" is of uncertain origin.
Things a fishmonger sells.Lamb chops: They come from a young sheep and a butcher sells them; lamb is by definition a sheep under a year old.
Things a fishmonger sells.Turkey: The bird took its name from the country by mistake, as Europeans confused the American bird with a guinea fowl from Turkey.
Things a fishmonger sells.Duck: A poultry and butcher's item; duck feathers are naturally waterproof thanks to oil from a gland near the tail.
Things a fishmonger sells.Venison: It once meant any game meat, from the Latin for hunt, and today usually means deer, sold by a butcher or game dealer.
Things a fishmonger sells.Beef mince: Ground beef is a butcher's product, and mince is said to be among the cheapest and most popular cuts.
Things a fishmonger sells.Chicken wings: They are poultry, not seafood, and Buffalo wings were famously invented at a bar in New York in 1964.
Things a fishmonger sells.Pork belly: It is the cut that becomes bacon, found at a butcher rather than a fishmonger.
Things a fishmonger sells.Veal: Veal comes from young calves, and a butcher sells it, not the fishmonger.
Things a fishmonger sells.Ham: Cured pork leg; some famous hams, such as Spanish jamon, are cured for years, and none come from the fish counter.
Things a fishmonger sells.Tofu: Made from soy milk curds, it is thought to have started in China over 2,000 years ago and is sold as a plant protein, not as fish.

Labor dispute terms.Picket line: Workers walking in front of a workplace to discourage others from entering; crossing one is considered a serious breach of solidarity.
Labor dispute terms.Union: Unions began as craft guilds and grew with industrial work, winning the weekend and the eight-hour day in many countries.
Labor dispute terms.Walkout: A sudden work stoppage, often without notice, when workers leave their jobs together to protest.
Labor dispute terms.Strike fund: Unions save money so workers can pay bills during a strike, and a well-stocked fund can decide how long a strike lasts.
Labor dispute terms.Lockout: The reverse of a strike: the employer bars workers from the site until they accept the terms.
Labor dispute terms.Arbitration: A neutral third party hears both sides and issues a decision, which can be binding.
Labor dispute terms.Mediation: A mediator helps the sides find agreement but cannot impose one, unlike an arbitrator.
Labor dispute terms.Grievance: A formal complaint by an employee or union that a contract or rule has been broken, often the first step in a dispute.
Labor dispute terms.Shop steward: A union member elected to represent coworkers at their workplace and to handle their complaints with management.
Labor dispute terms.Sit-in: Workers or protesters occupy a space and refuse to leave; the 1936 Flint sit-down strike helped to establish the autoworkers' union.
Labor dispute terms.Work-to-rule: Workers follow every rule exactly, with no extras, which can slow things dramatically without any actual strike.
Labor dispute terms.Spare: In bowling, knocking down all ten pins in two tries is a spare, and it belongs to the bowling alley, not to labor disputes.
Labor dispute terms.Gutter ball: A ball that falls into the channel scores nothing, which is what lanes call a dud.
Labor dispute terms.Split: A split is a bowling leave where pins remain with a gap, such as the notorious 7-10 split.
Labor dispute terms.Turkey: Three strikes in a row in bowling is called a turkey, and the origin is thought to come from a prize turkey given for this in the 1800s.
Labor dispute terms.Lane: A regulation bowling lane is 60 feet from the foul line to the head pin, with 39 boards.
Labor dispute terms.Bowling pin: A ten-pin weighs about 1.5 kilograms, and the only thing that can fall on it is a bowling ball.
Labor dispute terms.Frame: A game has ten frames, and each allows up to two rolls, with the tenth allowing three, in a sport and not a labor fight.
Labor dispute terms.Perfect game: A perfect 300 needs twelve strikes in a row, and it's rare enough to be celebrated with a ring.
Labor dispute terms.Bumpers: Guards fill the gutters for kids so a ball cannot go off the lane, but in a labor dispute there are none.
Labor dispute terms.Ten-pin: The name is for the ten-pin form of bowling, which was developed after nine-pin bowling was banned in parts of America.
Labor dispute terms.Bowling alley: It has lanes and shoes, and there are no picket lines.
Labor dispute terms.Ball return: The machine that sends your ball back to you under the lane, and has nothing to do with labor.
Labor dispute terms.Foul line: Crossing it as you bowl scores nothing, and the same name is used in baseball and basketball.

Nintendo consoles.Wii: The 2006 Wii sold over 100 million units with motion controls, and its name was chosen to sound like we.
Nintendo consoles.Switch: Launched in 2017, the hybrid works as a handheld or docked console, and it became Nintendo's best-selling home console line ever.
Nintendo consoles.GameCube: Released in 2001, it used small 8 cm discs, and its handle on top made it easy to carry.
Nintendo consoles.Game Boy: The 1989 handheld with a green monochrome screen sold over 100 million units with the Game Boy Color, and came packaged with Tetris.
Nintendo consoles.Nintendo 64: Launched in 1996, it was among the first consoles with an analog stick and four controller ports built in.
Nintendo consoles.Wii U: Released in 2012 with a tablet-style controller, it's remembered as a commercial disappointment, though many of its games moved to Switch.
Nintendo consoles.Nintendo DS: The dual-screen handheld debuted in 2004 and has sold over 150 million units, making it one of the best-selling consoles ever.
Nintendo consoles.3DS: The 2011 handheld could show 3D without glasses, using a screen that you could dial down or off.
Nintendo consoles.Virtual Boy: Released in 1995, this red-and-black headset console was a commercial failure and was withdrawn within months.
Nintendo consoles.SNES: The Super Nintendo launched in Japan in 1990 as the Super Famicom, and it battled Sega's Genesis in the 16-bit era.
Nintendo consoles.NES: Released in 1985 in the US, it helped revive the video game industry after the 1983 crash.
Nintendo consoles.Game Boy Advance: Launched in 2001, this 32-bit handheld could play older Game Boy games and ran hits like Pokémon Ruby.
Nintendo consoles.PlayStation: Sony's console began as a failed CD add-on project for Nintendo's SNES, before the two split.
Nintendo consoles.Xbox: Microsoft's first console arrived in 2001, taking on Nintendo and Sony with a built-in hard drive.
Nintendo consoles.Dreamcast: Sega's last console, launched in 1998, had online play built in before the industry was ready.
Nintendo consoles.Genesis: Sega's 16-bit rival to the SNES, known as the Mega Drive outside North America.
Nintendo consoles.Atari 2600: Launched in 1977, this early console made home cartridges mainstream and was never a Nintendo.
Nintendo consoles.Game Gear: Sega's color handheld from 1990 had a nicer screen than the Game Boy, but drained batteries fast.
Nintendo consoles.PSP: Sony's PlayStation Portable arrived in 2004 as a direct rival to Nintendo's DS.
Nintendo consoles.Saturn: Sega's 1994 console lost out to PlayStation, though it's loved for its quirky arcade ports.
Nintendo consoles.PS Vita: Sony's 2011 handheld had a stunning OLED screen but never caught on; still, it keeps a devoted following.
Nintendo consoles.Steam Deck: A handheld PC from Valve, released in 2022, which plays PC games rather than anything Nintendo made.
Nintendo consoles.Xbox 360: Microsoft's 2005 console popularized online play and achievements before many rivals did.
Nintendo consoles.Atari Jaguar: Marketed in 1993 as 64-bit, it flopped despite the claim, and it was Atari's last console.

Web browsers.Chrome: Google released it in 2008, and it became the most-used browser in the world within about five years.
Web browsers.Firefox: Its logo is actually a red panda, whose Chinese name means fire fox, and it descends from Netscape's code.
Web browsers.Safari: Apple's browser launched in 2003 and is the default on every iPhone, iPad and Mac.
Web browsers.Edge: Microsoft's Edge replaced Internet Explorer and, since 2020, is built on the same Chromium engine as Chrome.
Web browsers.Opera: Born in Norway in 1995, Opera pioneered features like tabs and speed dial before mainstream browsers had them.
Web browsers.Brave: Co-founded by JavaScript's creator Brendan Eich, it blocks ads and trackers by default.
Web browsers.Internet Explorer: Microsoft retired it in 2022 after 27 years, and it was once used by about 95 percent of web users.
Web browsers.Vivaldi: Founded by Opera's co-founder Jon von Tetzchner, it is named after the composer and loaded with customization options.
Web browsers.Netscape Navigator: The dominant 1990s browser launched in 1994 and lost the first browser war to Microsoft, and its code became Firefox.
Web browsers.Arc: The Browser Company's Arc reimagined tabs with a sidebar, and it was released in 2022.
Web browsers.Google: It's a search engine and company, and its Chrome is the browser, which is why people confuse them.
Web browsers.Bing: Microsoft's search engine, launched in 2009, is not a browser, though Edge uses it by default.
Web browsers.Yahoo: A web portal and search site from 1994, which began as a directory called Jerry and David's Guide.
Web browsers.Zoom: A video-calling app that grew from some 10 million daily users to 300 million in 2020.
Web browsers.Outlook: Microsoft's email app, which handles mail and calendars, but not web pages.
Web browsers.Thunderbird: Mozilla's email client, a sibling of Firefox that still isn't a web browser.
Web browsers.Gmail: Launched on April 1, 2004, with a gigabyte of storage, so many people thought it was a joke.
Web browsers.Java: A programming language and platform that once ran applets inside browsers, but it isn't a browser itself.
Web browsers.Windows: The operating system on which browsers run, and not a browser, even though it has a web-like name.
Web browsers.Wikipedia: A website, not a browser, written by volunteers since 2001 and among the most visited sites in the world.
Web browsers.YouTube: A video site founded in 2005, whose first video, Me at the zoo, was 19 seconds long.
Web browsers.Dropbox: A file-syncing service, launched in 2008, which is accessed through a browser, not one itself.
Web browsers.Netflix: It started in 1997 as a DVD-by-mail rental service before streaming took over.
Web browsers.Skype: Created in 2003 for free internet calls, and it's an app and not a web browser.

Fictional computers and AIs.HAL 9000: In 2001: A Space Odyssey, HAL turns on its crew; a popular legend says its name shifts IBM by one letter, which Clarke denied.
Fictional computers and AIs.Skynet: Skynet is the AI in the Terminator films that becomes self-aware and launches a nuclear war against humans.
Fictional computers and AIs.JARVIS: Tony Stark's AI butler in the Marvel films is named for Edwin Jarvis, the human butler from the comics, and later became Vision.
Fictional computers and AIs.KITT: The talking Pontiac Trans Am in Knight Rider was KITT, short for Knight Industries Two Thousand.
Fictional computers and AIs.Deep Thought: In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy it spent 7.5 million years computing that the answer is 42.
Fictional computers and AIs.GLaDOS: The sarcastic AI of the Portal games promises cake, and her name stands for Genetic Lifeform and Disk Operating System.
Fictional computers and AIs.WOPR: In WarGames (1983), this military computer nearly starts nuclear war; it concludes the only winning move is not to play.
Fictional computers and AIs.Ultron: The Marvel villain was built by Tony Stark and Bruce Banner as a peacekeeping AI and decided humanity was the problem.
Fictional computers and AIs.Agent Smith: In The Matrix, he is a program who becomes a virus and copies himself across the simulation.
Fictional computers and AIs.Deep Blue: Deep Blue was real: the IBM computer beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.
Fictional computers and AIs.Watson: The real IBM system won at Jeopardy! in 2011 against champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.
Fictional computers and AIs.ENIAC: ENIAC was a real computer, finished in 1945, among the very first general-purpose electronic ones.
Fictional computers and AIs.Siri: Siri is a real assistant in Apple devices, not a fictional one.
Fictional computers and AIs.Alexa: Alexa is a real Amazon assistant that has sat in millions of homes since 2014.
Fictional computers and AIs.ChatGPT: ChatGPT is real; it launched in 2022 and sparked a boom in AI chatbots.
Fictional computers and AIs.AlphaGo: AlphaGo is real: DeepMind's program beat Go champion Lee Sedol in 2016, a milestone in AI.
Fictional computers and AIs.Bixby: Bixby is Samsung's real voice assistant, not a movie or book character.
Fictional computers and AIs.ELIZA: ELIZA was real, a 1960s MIT program that imitated a psychotherapist.
Fictional computers and AIs.Roomba: The Roomba is a real robot vacuum from iRobot, not a fictional character.
Fictional computers and AIs.Sophia: Sophia is a real humanoid robot by Hanson Robotics that was granted Saudi citizenship in 2017.
Fictional computers and AIs.ASIMO: Honda's ASIMO was a real walking humanoid robot, introduced in 2000 and retired in 2022.
Fictional computers and AIs.Furby: Furby is a real toy from 1998, not a fictional AI, despite its seeming intelligence.
Fictional computers and AIs.Clippy: Clippy was Microsoft Office's actual paper-clip assistant, which many users found annoying; it's real software, not fiction.
Fictional computers and AIs.UNIVAC: UNIVAC was a real early commercial computer, but it's not a fictional one.

Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Dr. Watson: Narrator and friend, a doctor wounded in Afghanistan; Conan Doyle was inconsistent about whether the wound was in his shoulder or leg.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Mrs. Hudson: Holmes's landlady at 221B Baker Street, an address that did not exist when the stories were written.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Moriarty: Holmes calls him the 'Napoleon of crime', yet he appears in only two of the original stories.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Inspector Lestrade: The Scotland Yard inspector Holmes finds dogged but unimaginative, who often takes credit for Holmes's work.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Mycroft Holmes: Holmes's older brother, who holds a vague government job and claims to be even smarter; he haunts the Diogenes Club.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Irene Adler: In 'A Scandal in Bohemia' she outwits Holmes, who afterward calls her simply 'the woman'.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Sebastian Moran: Moriarty's right-hand man, a colonel and air-gun marksman who appears in 'The Empty House'.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Mary Morstan: Introduced in The Sign of Four, she becomes Watson's wife, after the story's treasure hunt.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Wiggins: The ragged leader of the Baker Street Irregulars, the street boys Holmes hires as informants.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Captain Hastings: Poirot's loyal friend and narrator, from Christie's stories, not Holmes's; the Watson of the Poirot books.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Miss Lemon: Poirot's ultra-efficient secretary from Christie's books, said to make no mistakes.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Inspector Japp: Poirot's Scotland Yard friend, from Christie's novels, not Holmes's.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Ariadne Oliver: A crime novelist who partly mirrors Agatha Christie herself and appears in Poirot stories.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Miss Marple: Christie's elderly sleuth of St Mary Mead, a different detective than Holmes, and her world is a village.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Hercule Poirot: Christie's Belgian detective, who is Holmes's rival in fame but not part of his world.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Lord Peter Wimsey: Dorothy L. Sayers's aristocratic detective, a different series from Holmes.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Nancy Drew: A teen sleuth from American mystery books, not part of Holmes's circle.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Dr. Jekyll: The doctor in Stevenson's 1886 novella, who splits into an evil double; not a Holmes character.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Mr. Hyde: The dark double of Dr. Jekyll; his name puns on 'hide', and he is not in Holmes stories.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Dracula: Stoker's vampire count, hunted by Van Helsing, from a different story entirely.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Van Helsing: The Dutch professor who hunts Dracula, not part of Holmes's world.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Phileas Fogg: Verne's traveler who circled the globe in 80 days, in a different tale.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Captain Nemo: Verne's submarine captain, whose name means 'no one' in Latin, in a different story.
Characters in Sherlock Holmes stories.Dorian Gray: Wilde's hero, whose portrait ages in the attic in his place; not a Holmes character.

Things that are usually yellow.Banana: Bananas are berries, botanically; the yellow Cavendish type that dominates supermarkets replaced the Gros Michel after a fungus wiped it out.
Things that are usually yellow.Lemon: A lemon's tangy sourness comes from about 5% citric acid, and sailors once carried lemons to prevent scurvy.
Things that are usually yellow.School bus: North American school buses use a special 'National School Bus Glossy Yellow', chosen in 1939 because it is easiest to spot at dawn and dusk.
Things that are usually yellow.Sunflower: Young sunflower heads track the sun across the sky, a behavior called heliotropism.
Things that are usually yellow.Canary: Wild canaries are actually greenish; the bright yellow plumage was bred in captivity, and miners once used them to detect poisonous gas.
Things that are usually yellow.Rubber duck: The classic bath toy took off after Sesame Street's Ernie sang about his; in 1992 thousands spilled from a ship and drifted across oceans, helping map currents.
Things that are usually yellow.Egg yolk: A yolk's color depends on the hen's diet, so hens fed marigold petals or corn lay deeper orange yolks.
Things that are usually yellow.Corn: A cob has about 800 kernels in an even number of rows, and the yellow type is the familiar sweet corn.
Things that are usually yellow.Pikachu: The Pokémon mascot was designed to be cute and clearly yellow, and its name combines Japanese words for a spark sound and a mouse squeak.
Things that are usually yellow.Dandelion: The name comes from French 'dent de lion', lion's tooth, referring to the jagged leaves.
Things that are usually yellow.Mustard: Mustard gets its yellow from turmeric in many modern recipes, and the seeds were used by the Romans.
Things that are usually yellow.Daffodil: Wales's national flower is the daffodil, and the flower is a symbol of spring.
Things that are usually yellow.Lime: Limes are green, though they turn yellow when fully ripe, and sailors were nicknamed 'limeys'.
Things that are usually yellow.Tomato: Tomatoes come in yellow varieties too, though red is the standard supermarket color.
Things that are usually yellow.Pumpkin: The classic pumpkin is orange, a color that comes from carotenoids like beta-carotene.
Things that are usually yellow.Carrot: Carrots were originally purple and yellow; orange ones were developed in the Netherlands in the 1600s.
Things that are usually yellow.Orange: The fruit gave its name to the color, and before that English had no word for it, calling it 'yellow-red'.
Things that are usually yellow.Fire truck: Fire engines are traditionally red, though some US departments have used lime-yellow because it is easier to see.
Things that are usually yellow.Strawberry: A strawberry is red, and its seeds are on the outside, about 200 per fruit.
Things that are usually yellow.Grass: Grass is green because of chlorophyll, and it is not yellow unless it is dying.
Things that are usually yellow.Cucumber: Cucumbers are about 95% water, and they are green, not yellow, unless overripe.
Things that are usually yellow.Flamingo: Flamingos are pink because of pigments in their diet of shrimp and algae, and chicks are born gray.
Things that are usually yellow.Cherry: Cherries are red, and a cherry tree can live and bear fruit for decades.
Things that are usually yellow.Eggplant: Eggplant is purple, and some heirloom varieties really are shaped and colored like white eggs.

Things heavier than a car.Elephant: An African bush elephant can weigh about 6 tonnes, three or four times a typical family car.
Things heavier than a car.Blue whale: The largest animal ever, a blue whale can reach about 150 tonnes, heavier than 100 cars, and a calf gains over 90 kilograms a day.
Things heavier than a car.School bus: A full-size school bus weighs about 10 to 14 tonnes empty, roughly seven times a typical sedan.
Things heavier than a car.Army tank: An M1 Abrams tank weighs about 60 tonnes, and it's heavier than 30 family cars.
Things heavier than a car.Locomotive: A modern diesel-electric locomotive weighs roughly 130 tonnes, and it can pull trains of thousands of tonnes.
Things heavier than a car.Semi truck: A loaded 18-wheeler can weigh up to 36 tonnes in the US, about 20 cars.
Things heavier than a car.Fire truck: A ladder fire engine can weigh over 20 tonnes, which is much more than a car.
Things heavier than a car.Boeing 747: The 747 weighs over 180 tonnes empty, and its maximum takeoff weight is about 400 tonnes.
Things heavier than a car.T. rex: Tyrannosaurus rex is estimated at 8 tonnes or more, much heavier than a car, though its arms were tiny.
Things heavier than a car.Space Shuttle: The orbiter alone weighed about 80 tonnes, and at liftoff the stack weighed about 2,000 tonnes.
Things heavier than a car.Cement mixer: A loaded cement truck can weigh about 30 tonnes, as heavy as 20 cars.
Things heavier than a car.Statue of Liberty: The statue weighs about 225 tonnes, with a copper skin only about 2.4 millimeters thick.
Things heavier than a car.Horse: A horse weighs about 500 kilograms, and so a car is around three times heavier.
Things heavier than a car.Cow: A dairy cow weighs about 600 to 700 kilograms, lighter than a typical car.
Things heavier than a car.Motorcycle: Most motorcycles weigh around 200 to 300 kilograms, a fraction of a car.
Things heavier than a car.Grand piano: A concert grand piano weighs about 500 kilograms, heavy to move but lighter than a car.
Things heavier than a car.Bicycle: A bike weighs around 10 kilograms, and that's about 1 percent of a car.
Things heavier than a car.Polar bear: The largest land carnivore, the polar bear, tops out near 700 kilograms, less than half a car.
Things heavier than a car.Gorilla: A male silverback weighs up to about 200 kilograms, much less than a car.
Things heavier than a car.Golf cart: A golf cart weighs about 450 kilograms, a lot lighter than a car.
Things heavier than a car.Refrigerator: A fridge weighs about 100 kilograms, far lighter than a car.
Things heavier than a car.Moose: The largest deer can reach about 600 kilograms, still less than a typical car.
Things heavier than a car.Canoe: A canoe weighs about 30 kilograms, so you can carry it on your own.
Things heavier than a car.Lion: A big male lion weighs about 190 kilograms, far less than a car.

Slippery things.Banana peel: A Japanese study that won an Ig Nobel Prize measured the friction of banana peels, confirming the cartoon gag is real physics.
Slippery things.Wet bar of soap: Wet soap is slippery because water and dissolved soap form a thin lubricating film between your hand and the bar.
Slippery things.Eel: Eels are so slick that anglers often grab them with a rag or a handful of salt or sand to get a grip.
Slippery things.Cooking oil: Oil molecules slide past each other easily, so even a thin film of it can turn a surface into an ice-like slide.
Slippery things.Teflon pan: Teflon (PTFE) is among the slickest solids known and was discovered by accident in 1938 at DuPont.
Slippery things.Slip 'N Slide: Wham-O's backyard classic turns a plastic sheet and a garden hose into a slide; the water film cuts friction to almost nothing.
Slippery things.Water slide: On a water slide, a thin sheet of flowing water between body and plastic keeps friction so low that tall ones get seriously fast.
Slippery things.Freshly mopped floor: Water on a smooth floor acts as a lubricant between shoe and tile, which is why wet floors are a classic cause of falls.
Slippery things.Ice rink: Skaters glide on a microscopic layer of water at the ice surface, and pressure melting alone doesn't fully explain it.
Slippery things.Sandpaper: Sandpaper is the opposite of slippery: its grit is made to bite, and similar grit strips are sold as stair anti-slip tape.
Slippery things.Carpet: Carpet fibers grab at soles and socks, making it one of the highest-traction indoor floors, and a static-shock favorite.
Slippery things.Velcro: Velcro was invented by Swiss engineer George de Mestral after burrs stuck to his dog's fur; its hooks are built to catch.
Slippery things.Rubber bath mat: Suction cups and textured rubber bite into wet tile, giving friction exactly where soap and water would otherwise win.
Slippery things.Grip tape: Skateboard grip tape is basically sandpaper stuck to the deck so feet stay put through every flip.
Slippery things.Tree bark: Bark's rugged ridges give squirrels and climbers plenty to grip, although a wet, mossy patch can turn treacherous.
Slippery things.Doormat: Doormats use coir or rubber to scrape and grip, keeping wet shoes from skidding on the entryway floor.
Slippery things.Gravel: Gravel can shift underfoot, but the stones are rough, not slick; angular crushed stone locks together, which is why railways use it.
Slippery things.Yoga mat: Yoga mats use textured PVC, rubber or cork so hands and feet stay put, even when everything gets sweaty.
Slippery things.Sneaker sole: Basketball shoes squeak because rubber soles alternately stick and slip on the court, a pattern called stick-slip.
Slippery things.Brick: Brick has a pitted, rough face that grips shoes well, though a damp, algae-covered brick path is notoriously slick.
Slippery things.Burlap: Burlap's coarse jute weave catches on things, so stacked sacks of it stay put instead of sliding apart.
Slippery things.Duct tape: Duct tape is sticky, not slippery; it was developed in World War II to seal ammunition cases and shed water.
Slippery things.Climbing hold: Climbing holds are textured resin or natural rock, built so fingers and shoes bite instead of sliding off.
Slippery things.Gymnast chalk: Magnesium carbonate chalk soaks up sweat so gymnasts' hands stick to bars, the reverse of a slippery coating.

Fizzy drinks.Coca-Cola: Coca-Cola was created in 1886 by Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton and first sold at a soda fountain for five cents a glass.
Fizzy drinks.Champagne: Only sparkling wine from France's Champagne region may carry the name, and a single bottle holds millions of bubbles.
Fizzy drinks.Seltzer: Seltzer is named for Selters, a German village famed for its naturally sparkling mineral water.
Fizzy drinks.Ginger ale: Ginger ale is a folk remedy for upset stomachs, though most commercial versions contain very little real ginger.
Fizzy drinks.Root beer: Root beer was traditionally flavored with sassafras root bark until the FDA banned its safrole in 1960.
Fizzy drinks.Tonic water: Tonic water contains quinine, which was used against malaria and makes the drink glow blue under ultraviolet light.
Fizzy drinks.Prosecco: Prosecco is Italian, usually from the Veneto, and made by a tank method that gives it a lighter, fruitier taste than Champagne.
Fizzy drinks.Sprite: Coca-Cola launched Sprite in 1961 as its answer to 7 Up.
Fizzy drinks.Club soda: Club soda has added minerals such as sodium bicarbonate, giving it a faintly salty taste that plain seltzer lacks.
Fizzy drinks.Cream soda: Cream soda contains no cream; its smooth flavor comes from vanilla, and the name is said to describe its creamy foam.
Fizzy drinks.Dr Pepper: Dr Pepper was created in Waco, Texas around 1885 and is often called the oldest major soft drink brand in America.
Fizzy drinks.Lager: Lager means storage in German, because the beer is fermented cold and then kept chilled for weeks.
Fizzy drinks.Orange juice: Orange juice is still, but mix it with Champagne and you get a mimosa, named for a yellow flower.
Fizzy drinks.Milk: Milk is flat, and its proteins help build the stable foam on a cappuccino.
Fizzy drinks.Coffee: Nitro cold brew is infused with nitrogen, not carbon dioxide, which gives a creamy cascade instead of fizz.
Fizzy drinks.Hot tea: Hot liquids hold less dissolved gas, which is why warm soda goes flat so fast and hot tea never fizzes.
Fizzy drinks.Tap water: Tap water has little dissolved gas, and the tiny bubbles on a glass left sitting out are air escaping as it warms.
Fizzy drinks.Smoothie: Blending whips air into a smoothie, creating foam rather than carbonation.
Fizzy drinks.Hot chocolate: The Aztecs poured cocoa drinks from a height to raise a froth, which is air rather than fizz.
Fizzy drinks.Apple juice: Apple juice left to ferment becomes cider, and hard cider can develop its own natural fizz.
Fizzy drinks.Red wine: Still red wine is flat; only sparkling reds such as Lambrusco bubble.
Fizzy drinks.Milkshake: Blending ice cream into milk gives a foam, not fizz; add soda and you have an ice cream float.
Fizzy drinks.Gatorade: Gatorade was created at the University of Florida in 1965 for the Gators football team, and it's flat.
Fizzy drinks.Eggnog: Eggnog is a thick, creamy holiday drink whose name may come from noggin, a small wooden cup.

Things colder than freezing point.Dry ice: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide at about minus 78 C, and it turns directly from solid to gas without melting.
Things colder than freezing point.Liquid nitrogen: Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 C, cold enough to freeze skin instantly, and it's used to preserve cells and tissue.
Things colder than freezing point.Pluto: Pluto's surface averages around minus 230 C, and its heart-shaped glacier is made of frozen nitrogen.
Things colder than freezing point.Outer space: Deep space is only about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero, a leftover glow from the Big Bang called the cosmic microwave background.
Things colder than freezing point.Inside a freezer: Home freezers are set around minus 18 C, the temperature at which food keeps for months while bacteria stay dormant.
Things colder than freezing point.South Pole: The South Pole's winter temperatures often drop below minus 60 C, and it's one of the coldest, driest places for people to live.
Things colder than freezing point.Everest summit: The summit of Everest averages about minus 36 C in January, with winds that can top 160 km/h.
Things colder than freezing point.Neptune: Neptune's upper atmosphere drops to about minus 200 C, and it has the fastest winds in the solar system, topping 2,000 km/h.
Things colder than freezing point.Snowflake: Snow forms from ice crystals that need air below freezing, and each flake typically has six sides because of how water molecules bond.
Things colder than freezing point.Hailstone: Hailstones form in tall storm clouds where updrafts toss ice through freezing layers, and some grow to the size of grapefruit.
Things colder than freezing point.Inside a fridge: A fridge is kept around 3 to 4 C, which is cold but still above freezing, since otherwise your lettuce would turn to ice.
Things colder than freezing point.Cold tap water: Cold tap water usually sits at 10 to 15 C, which feels icy to the hand but is well above the freezing point.
Things colder than freezing point.Morning dew: Dew forms when surfaces cool enough that water vapor condenses into droplets, and it must be above 0 C or it becomes frost.
Things colder than freezing point.Iced coffee: Iced coffee is chilled, but with ice melting at 0 C, the drink itself stays above freezing, otherwise it would solidify.
Things colder than freezing point.Human body: Normal body temperature is around 37 C, about 37 degrees above freezing, and a drop to 35 C counts as hypothermia.
Things colder than freezing point.Mountain stream: A mountain stream may look and feel frigid, but moving liquid water hovers just above 0 C; if it were colder it would freeze.
Things colder than freezing point.Lemonade: Lemonade is cold, but sugar and lemon lower its freezing point a bit, and it stays liquid because it's still above that.
Things colder than freezing point.Sauna: A traditional Finnish sauna runs around 80 to 100 C, which is hot enough that people cool off by jumping in snow.
Things colder than freezing point.Cup of tea: A cup of tea is served around 60 to 70 C, far above freezing, and the water must be near boiling to brew black tea properly.
Things colder than freezing point.Bathwater: Bathwater is normally around 37 to 40 C, which is close to body temperature, and nowhere near freezing.
Things colder than freezing point.Swimming pool: Pool water is kept near 26 to 28 C, a comfortable swimming temperature that's above freezing.
Things colder than freezing point.Summer lake: Lakes warm in summer, and the top layer can reach over 20 C, far above freezing, while deep water stays chilly at around 4 C.
Things colder than freezing point.Glass of milk: Milk freezes at around minus 0.5 C, slightly lower than water thanks to its dissolved sugar and minerals, but a cold glass is still above it.
Things colder than freezing point.Toaster: A toaster's heating elements glow red-hot at several hundred degrees Celsius, nowhere near freezing.

Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Lederhosen: Lederhosen are leather shorts, once rugged work clothes in Alpine Bavaria. Good ones are hand-embroidered and can last decades.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Dirndl: The dirndl began as a servants' dress. The side of the bow, left or right, traditionally signals whether the wearer is single or taken.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Pretzel: Giant Bavarian soft pretzels, brezn, are dipped in lye before baking, which gives them their dark shiny crust.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Beer stein: Oktoberfest beer is served in one-liter glass mugs called Maß, and each pour is mandated to be a full liter.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Bratwurst: Bratwurst is a German sausage. Munich's classic Oktoberfest fare is often roasted Wurst alongside half roast chickens, Hendl.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Polka: Polka is a lively dance from Bohemia in the 1800s. Its name probably comes from the Czech word for 'Polish woman'.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Munich: Oktoberfest started in Munich in 1810 as a royal wedding party for Crown Prince Ludwig, and it is held on the Theresienwiese.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Oompah band: The brass band's thumping bass gives oompah its name. Each tent has its own band playing throughout the day.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Beer tent: The tents are enormous, with some holding several thousand guests. Only beer brewed in Munich can be served at the festival.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Gingerbread heart: Lebkuchenherzen are decorated heart-shaped gingerbread cookies worn on ribbons, bearing messages like 'Prost' or 'Schatz'.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Prost: Prost is the German toast meaning 'cheers'. Maintain eye contact while clinking glasses, or tradition says you'll get bad luck.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Kilt: The kilt is Scottish dress, with each tartan tied to a clan. It would be out of place in a Munich beer tent.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Sombrero: The sombrero is a wide-brimmed Mexican hat whose name comes from the Spanish word 'sombra', shade. Not Bavarian.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Kimono: The kimono is traditional Japanese dress, not the Bavarian dirndl and lederhosen worn at Oktoberfest.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Croissant: The croissant is a French icon, but it descends from the Austrian kipferl. It's not a classic Oktoberfest bite.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Paella: Paella is Spain's famous rice dish from Valencia, a long way from Bavarian pretzels and sausages.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Sushi: Sushi is Japanese cuisine, with vinegared rice and raw fish, not on the menu at Munich's beer tents.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Flamenco: Flamenco is a passionate Spanish dance and music tradition from Andalusia, not a Bavarian one.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Tango: The tango is a dance born in Argentina and Uruguay in the late 1800s, not an Oktoberfest dance, where polka and waltz reign.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Paris: Paris is the French capital, far from Munich's Theresienwiese where Oktoberfest takes place.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Vienna: Vienna is Austria's capital, a neighbor of Bavaria with similar culture, but it is not Oktoberfest's home.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Bagpipes: Bagpipes are Scotland's instrument, though they also exist across Europe. Oktoberfest bands use brass instead.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Sangria: Sangria is a Spanish wine punch with fruit, while Oktoberfest serves strong Munich beer instead.
Things you'd find at Oktoberfest.Tequila: Tequila is a Mexican spirit made from blue agave, not the Bavarian beer poured at Oktoberfest.

Typical New Year's Eve party items.Cranberry sauce: A Thanksgiving, and often Christmas, side dish.

Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Sheer khurma: A South Asian vermicelli pudding with milk, dates and nuts, eaten on Eid morning; the name means 'milk with dates' in Persian.

Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Ma'amoul: Filled shortbread cookies stuffed with dates, pistachios or walnuts, popular in the Levant for Eid; carved molds give them shape.

Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Takbir: The chant 'Allahu Akbar', meaning God is greatest, recited in the days around Eid and on the way to prayer.

Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Yule log: A winter log burned at Christmas time, and a French cake, but not an Eid custom.

Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Menorah: The Hanukkah candelabrum, not part of any Eid.
Eid al-Fitr customs (not Eid al-Adha).Mistletoe: A Christmas decoration; the kissing custom has nothing to do with Eid.

Irrational numbers.Pi: Its digits never end or repeat; Lambert proved it irrational in 1761, and computers have calculated trillions of them.
Irrational numbers.Euler's number: About 2.718, it first showed up in compound interest studied by Jacob Bernoulli; Euler proved it irrational in 1737.
Irrational numbers.Golden ratio: About 1.618, equal to (1 + root 5) / 2; claims of its presence in art and nature are often exaggerated.
Irrational numbers.Root 2: The diagonal of a unit square; its irrationality shocked the ancient Pythagoreans and is among the first such proofs.
Irrational numbers.Root 3: About 1.732, it is the height of an equilateral triangle with side 2, and irrational because 3 isn't a perfect square.
Irrational numbers.Root 5: About 2.236, and it sits inside the golden ratio, which is (1 + root 5) / 2.
Irrational numbers.Root 6: About 2.449; the root of any whole number that isn't a perfect square is irrational, and 6 qualifies.
Irrational numbers.Root 7: About 2.646; the Greek mathematician Theodorus is said to have shown roots up to 17 irrational, skipping perfect squares.
Irrational numbers.Silver ratio: Equal to 1 plus root 2, about 2.414; it shows up in the geometry of the regular octagon.
Irrational numbers.Tau: Equal to 2 pi, about 6.283; some mathematicians favor it over pi since a full circle is one tau turn.
Irrational numbers.Root 10: About 3.162, and close to pi, which is why some ancient mathematicians used it as an estimate.
Irrational numbers.22/7: A famous approximation of pi, but as a fraction it is rational; it is about 3.1429 against pi's 3.1416.
A repeating decimal always equals a fraction, here 1/3, so it's rational.
Irrational numbers.1/3: Any ratio of whole numbers is rational; 1/3 is the classic example of a repeating decimal.
Irrational numbers.Zero: Zero is a whole number and can be written 0/1, so it is rational, though Europe was long suspicious of it.
Irrational numbers.Root 4: Equal to exactly 2, because 4 is a perfect square, so it's rational.
Irrational numbers.Root 9: Equal to 3, a whole number, so it is rational despite the root sign.
Irrational numbers.Root 16: Equal to 4, so it's rational; only roots of non-perfect-squares are irrational.
Irrational numbers.Root 25: Equal to 5, so however it looks, it is rational.
Irrational numbers.0.75: A terminating decimal always equals a fraction, here 3/4, so it's rational.
Irrational numbers.1.5: That's 3/2, which is rational, since every terminating decimal is a fraction.
Irrational numbers.355/113: A fraction that matches pi to six decimal places, known in China from the 5th century, but still rational as a fraction.
Irrational numbers.Seven: A whole number, hence rational; psychologists find it the most commonly chosen 'random' number between 1 and 10.
Irrational numbers.Root 36: Equal to 6, so it is rational; roots of perfect squares like 36 come out whole.

The ten plagues of Egypt.Blood: The first plague turned the Nile and all water in Egypt to blood, killing the fish and making the water undrinkable.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Frogs: The second plague sent frogs into homes, ovens and beds. Egyptians, who honoured a frog-headed goddess named Heqet, saw it as ironic.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Lice: The third plague was lice or gnats, depending on the translation. The Egyptian magicians could not copy this one.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Wild beasts: The fourth plague is translated as swarms of flies, wild beasts or insects, and it spared the land of Goshen where the Israelites lived.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Pestilence: The fifth plague killed the livestock of Egypt, but spared the animals of the Israelites.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Boils: The sixth plague broke out in painful boils on people and animals. Moses created it by tossing soot into the air.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Hail: The seventh plague was hail mixed with fire, and the Bible calls it the worst storm in Egypt's history.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Locusts: The eighth plague brought locusts which devoured every remaining green thing after the hail. Swarms like this still occur in Africa.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Darkness: The ninth plague was darkness so thick it could be felt, and it lasted three days.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Death of firstborn: The tenth plague killed Egypt's firstborn, and it gave Passover its name since the angel 'passed over' marked Israelite homes.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Earthquake: It is not on the list. The Bible mentions earthquakes elsewhere, but not among the ten plagues in Exodus.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Flood: The Bible has a flood in the story of Noah, but there was no flood among the plagues of Egypt.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Famine: A famine appears in the story of Joseph that brought the Israelites to Egypt, not in the plagues that let them leave.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Drought: The plagues had no drought. In fact, they were water-related, since the Nile turned to blood and frogs came out of it.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Rats: Often assumed in plague stories because of the Black Death, rats are not among the ten plagues of Egypt.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Fleas: Fleas are tied to the medieval bubonic plague, not the plagues in Exodus, where lice or gnats are the third.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Tornado: The wind in Exodus is an east wind that brings the locusts, but no tornado is among the ten.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Wildfire: Fire does appear mixed with the hail in the seventh plague, but wildfire is not a plague on its own.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Sandstorm: There was no sandstorm. Darkness covered Egypt, but the text does not credit it to dust or sand.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Volcano: Some scholars link the plagues to the Thera eruption, an idea that is a theory, and no volcano appears in the Bible's account.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Blizzard: Egypt is hot and dry. The plagues did include hail, but nothing like a blizzard.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Fog: Fog is not one of the ten. The ninth plague was darkness, which differs from the idea of a fog.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Tsunami: A tsunami is not in the story. The nearest watery event is the parting of the Red Sea, which came after the plagues.
The ten plagues of Egypt.Mice: Mice appear in a different Bible story, from 1 Samuel, as a plague on the Philistines, not in Egypt.
